title: On Christmas, God Shook Up the World
summary: Advent is waiting for something that not everyone can see. Advent is preparing to receive a gift that not everyone wants.
summary_zh: 降临节正在等待一些不是每个人都能看到的东西。Advent正准备接受一份并非所有人都想要的礼物。
title_zh: 在圣诞节，上帝震撼了世界
content: Read For thus says the LORD of hosts: Yet once more, in a little while, I will shake the heavens and the earth and the sea and the dry land. And I will shake all nations, so that the treasures of all nations shall come in, and I will fill this house with glory, says the LORD of hosts. (Hag. 2:6–7) Reflect When this prophecy came to Haggai in 520 BC, did anyone imagine that God would shake up the world with a baby born to humble parents in Bethlehem? Or that “a little while” would be more than 500 years later? Yet if Advent teaches us anything, it’s that the Lord works according to his own schedule and doesn’t act as we expect. His timeline may not align with ours, but in the passage of centuries we experience his mercy. We read in 2 Peter 3:9, “The Lord is not slow to fulfill his promise as some count slowness, but is patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance.” The Lord works according to his own schedule and doesn’t act as we expect. In Hebrews 12:26, the writer expands on this relationship between patience and judgment by quoting Haggai 2. The shaking is a kind of sifting, like the sand separated from jewels in a strainer. The Lord shakes the world to sift out anyone who doesn’t worship that baby born in Bethlehem. Because even as a helpless babe, he is the King of kings and Lord of lords who will reign forever. In Jesus we see “the radiance of the glory of God and the exact imprint of his nature,” the One who “upholds the universe by the word of his power” (Heb. 1:3). One day, after a little while, that baby would grow up and exercise his power in the most unexpected way. He would submit to death, even on a cross. The day he died on Calvary, the temple curtain was torn in two. An earthquake shook the city. Rocks split at the Place of a Skull (Matt. 27:32, 51). That helpless man, bloodied and beaten, commanded more authority than anyone else had realized—including the power to judge his judges. The Roman officer who commanded 100 confessed, “Truly this was the Son of God!” (v. 54). Those who don’t follow suit will be sifted. But the shed blood of the only Son of God has the power to forgive the sins of all who repent. By this sacrifice, believers will receive a “kingdom that cannot be shaken” (Heb. 12:28). To this kingdom all the treasures of the nations will accrue, as Haggai foresaw with the temple filled by God’s glory. God did this for the Hebrews when he delivered them from slavery. They plundered the Egyptians (Ex. 12:36). And he’ll do it again when he delivers the world from death, as the kings of the earth bring their glory to the temple in the new Jerusalem (Rev. 21:24). The shed blood of the only Son of God has the power to forgive the sins of all who repent. These kings will follow a path already trod by the wise men of the east, who tracked the star to baby Jesus. From the nations they brought their treasures—gold, frankincense, and myrrh. The purported king, Herod, could only see a threat. But these wise men fell down and worshiped the baby still nursing with his mother, Mary (Matt. 2:11). Do you see the power and the glory concealed from the world while contained in that baby? Do you see in him a King whose love for sinners kept him nailed to the cross? Advent is waiting for something that not everyone can see. Advent is preparing to receive a gift that not everyone wants. Advent is enduring an unstable world with hope because an unshakable kingdom is coming—in a little while. Respond How might the Lord’s seeming lack of action express his patience for you? How could you help your non-Christian friends and family see the glory in Jesus this Advent season?

title: Midlife Is a Crossroads, Not a Crisis
summary: In ‘Good News for Midlife,’ Jared Wilson reminds us to embrace our midlife crossroads, find new meaning in service to others, and let this season be an opportunity to discover grace upon grace in Jesus.
summary_zh: 在《中年好消息》（ Good News for Midlife ）一书中，贾里德·威尔逊（ Jared Wilson ）提醒我们要拥抱中年十字路口，寻找为他人服务的新意义，让这个季节成为在耶稣身上发现恩典的机会。
title_zh: 中年是一个十字路口，而不是危机
content: Last year, I was sitting with an early twentysomething grad student in our church. He said he was looking for an older man to mentor him, and I started thinking through our godly, wise men in their 50s and 60s. He stopped me and clarified: He was asking me to mentor him. “Wait, you think I’m old?!” I’m 42, and to be fair, I’ve been told I’m an “old soul” my whole life. Some have wondered aloud if I was born old. While I still don’t feel old, I’ll admit this new and strange season has spurred me to go looking for wisdom. I’ll tell you, reading about midlife is depressing. According to studies, happiness in life follows a U-shaped curve. Our self-reported happiness starts high in childhood, then decreases into adolescence and further into early adulthood. It bottoms out somewhere around age 46—smack in the center of middle age—before beginning to rise again and steadily increasing into our twilight years. Further, studies have shown that depression and anxiety also are highest around the age of 45. Despite all the bad news, Good News for Midlife: Navigating Middle Age with Guts and Grace was encouraging. Writing from his early 50s, Jared Wilson, associate pastor of pastoral ministry at Midwestern Baptist Theological Seminary, understands the challenges of midlife but also provides refreshing hope for those of us finding our own way through. Understand Midlife Most definitions place “middle age” as 40 to 60, but it’s probably more accurate to describe midlife in terms of its demands and responsibilities. For me, it looks something like this: I still feel energetic, but it takes far longer to recover from lost sleep, injuries, and travel. My kids are now teenagers, and some days, I only see them for a half hour. Our grocery bill is three times our first mortgage. Our parents are in their 70s and now need more support from us than we need from them. I think I’m still in touch with modern culture, but my kids assure me I’m not. I may have 40-plus years left, but it sure feels like most of my life is now behind me. Most deeply, I’m frequently reflecting on life’s disappointments and griefs, wondering if I should have done this or that differently. This is middle life. We’re too young to feel old. But we’re also too old to feel young. Wilson, who writes specifically for men entering or inhabiting these decades, acknowledges all these challenges. “But,” he writes, “while this season presents unique challenges . . . midlife also presents exciting opportunities to trust Jesus for personal, marital, and spiritual flourishing” (xi). Thankfully, Wilson helps us reframe the demands and opportunities of middle age not as a necessary crisis but as a critical crossroads . Crossroads, Not Crisis For almost 60 years, pop culture has made “midlife” nearly synonymous with “crisis.” The phrase comes from psychoanalyst Elliott Jaques’s 1965 essay “ Death and the Mid-Life Crisis ” and has been repeated across dozens of books ever since. (There’s even a board game called Mid-Life Crisis, where players aim to accumulate wealth and avoid landing on bankruptcy, divorce, and nervous breakdown.) This is middle life. We’re too young to feel old. But we’re also too old to feel young. Fortunately, recent studies suggest fewer than 20 percent of Americans experience a full-on crisis in these middle decades. Despite this, many of us face a unique temptation to flee from responsibility or forge some entirely new life. Wilson puts it poignantly: “Whether you’re in a crisis or not, at midlife you’re at a crossroads” (16). At this crossroads, we see down one path the allure of individualism and freedom from responsibility. We might simply call this path the road of empty promises. As the proverbs say, it seems right, but in the end, it leads to death (Prov. 14:12). The second path is one of embracing reality, stepping deeper into relationship, and trusting the goodness of God. This road offers no promises other than the hardships of real life. But it’s also where we

title: Avoid the Trap of Bitterness
summary: Joseph avoids the trap of bitterness. And you can too, if you follow these three steps.
summary_zh: 约瑟避免了痛苦的陷阱。如果你遵循这三个步骤，你也可以这样做。
title_zh: 避开苦涩的陷阱
content: Imagine the people closest to you betray you. It’s your trust in them that lets them get close enough to hurt you so terribly. Now, imagine that this betrayal completely upends your life for years . Everything that made your life good—your family, your home, your safety—is violently taken from you. Now imagine years bleed into decades. Your life spirals into ever more pain and isolation. And every jab of hurt leads you to agonize over the initial wound: None of this would have happened if it weren’t for them. How could they do this? However, in the last few years, your fortunes have turned around. From the slums, you’re suddenly lifted to a vaulted position of power. People no longer take advantage of you but try to stay in your good graces. It doesn’t wash all the bitter memories away, but it’s something. And then, lo and behold, who happens to come before you but them . Your cruel betrayers are there, groveling, asking you for help. How would you feel? What would you do? If you haven’t picked up on it yet, this is the story of Joseph from Genesis. Sold into slavery by his brothers, Joseph walks through much injustice and suffering before being catapulted into the most powerful office in Egypt, second only to Pharaoh. And when his brothers come cringing toward him in the end, certain that Joseph will use his power to pay them back, Joseph responds with unexpected mercy, generosity, and warmth (Gen. 50:15–21) . How? Joseph avoids the trap of bitterness. And you can too, if you follow these three steps. 1. Understand Bitterness Bitterness is revealed in our emotions (coldness, anger, resentment, suspicion, revulsion), but it begins in our will. We choose bitterness when we believe that for justice or fairness to be preserved, the offender must be punished in some way. We may even claim to forgive, but in our heart of hearts, we fear that forgiveness comes at the expense of justice. So, you give your spouse the silent treatment, you cut your parents off, you make life difficult for your kids. Joseph avoids bitterness by trusting that God is the One who takes care of justice. When his brothers beg for mercy, Joseph replies, “Do not fear, for am I in the place of God?” (Gen. 50:19). Joseph knows it isn’t his place to deal out the judgment only God can give. The first step in avoiding bitterness is letting God take care of final justice (Rom. 12:14–21). Bitterness feels like a solution to the problem, but it isn’t. It’s trying to solve one sin with another sin. Which is why we’re commanded unequivocally to repent of bitterness, full stop (Eph. 4:31). We’re never told bitterness is an acceptable method to coerce repentance or pursue justice, or is permissible until the other person apologizes and makes restitution. Reconciliation requires two people who are willing. But to repent of bitterness only requires one. Bitterness feels like a solution to the problem, but it isn’t. It’s trying to solve one sin with another sin. Bitterness isn’t the path to justice—only to more bitterness. Using bitterness to pursue justice is like using a hatchet to build a house, confident it’ll work just like a hammer. 2. Unmask Bitterness We’re called to be so absolute and unqualified in rejecting bitterness because of its penchant to spread. It’s a “root” (Heb. 12:15) that will only grow and become more difficult to uproot as time goes on. Plucking up a sapling is easy; removing an oak tree isn’t. Soon, the bitterness you feel toward Person A will make you more prone to taking offense at Person B and more sensitive to Person C. Soon, you become an angry person who holds grudges. It’s a root that “defiles many.” Bitterness is hard to detect initially because it hides so effectively behind a mask of morality. The bitter person “blesses himself in his heart, saying, ‘I shall be safe, though I walk in the stubbornness of my heart’” (Deut. 29:19). In other words, “I’m not wrong, they are! They’re the ones who hurt me!” It not only immediately puts you into a

title: Build a Culture of Evangelism
summary: Matt Smethurst and Ligon Duncan discuss how pastors can build a culture of evangelism by modeling gospel conversations, equipping church members to share their faith, and making evangelism a natural part of church life.
summary_zh: 马特·斯梅瑟斯特（ Matt Smethurst ）和利贡·邓肯（ Ligon Duncan ）讨论了牧师如何通过模仿福音对话，装备教会成员分享他们的信仰，并使传福音成为教会生活的自然组成部分来建立传福音的文化。
title_zh: 建立传福音的文化
content: How can pastors help their churches become more evangelistic without relying on another program? Matt Smethurst and Ligon Duncan discuss what it takes to build a culture where sharing the gospel becomes a normal part of church life. title: Train Women to Teach the Bible: A 4-Week Plan
summary: Bible studies are the heartbeat of women’s ministries in many churches. But where do we find teachers?
summary_zh: 圣经学习是许多教会中妇女事工的心跳。但是我们在哪里可以找到老师？
title_zh: 培训女性教导圣经： 4周计划
content: Bible studies are the heartbeat of women’s ministries in many churches. More and more churches have come to prefer live teaching over video studies . But this can present a challenge for women’s ministry directors: Where do we find teachers? Bible teachers don’t come ready-made. We have to raise them up through training. Whether women have never taught the Scriptures before or are building on previous experience, we can help them grow and gain confidence in “rightly handling the word of truth” (2 Tim. 2:15) through careful instruction and practice. To equip women in my church to teach, I helped develop a four-session course. Here’s how we developed and implemented this training. Get Organized I first recruited two women with experience teaching the Bible, and together we prepared ourselves as instructors by taking the online Simeon Trust First Principles for Women course. We then personalized the principles we learned to fit our training goals for other women in our church. Since there are different strategies for approaching various genres of Scripture, the first time we held this course, we chose to train women on how to teach an epistle. We selected 1 Peter as our text and assigned each group a passage to work on throughout the course. For example, Group 1 had 1 Peter 1:1–12, Group 2 had 1:13–21, and Group 3 had 4:12–19. We used 5:1–11 as a common passage that we studied as a whole group. In subsequent courses, we chose other genres of Scripture: narrative using passages from a Gospel and wisdom/poetry using a psalm. Bible teachers don’t come ready-made. We have to raise them up through training. We promoted the training with a clear purpose: to help participants grow in their ability to understand and teach God’s Word. We spelled out our expectations: attending all four sessions, completing homework, and teaching a 10-minute message to peers. Individual attention in training is key, so we assigned each participant to a small group of three to six women with a leader. The leader gave feedback on homework and answered questions. Teach the Course Here’s what we covered each week, including teaching content, small-group work, and homework assignments. Week 1: Foundations of Study After sharing two foundational truths about the Bible—Scripture is God-breathed (2 Tim. 3:16–17) and Scripture is alive and active, changing us as we study it (Heb. 4:12)—we taught three principles. First, we never add to or subtract from what’s written in the Word (Deut. 4:2; 1 Cor. 4:6; Rev. 22:18–19). A Bible text isn’t a jumping-off point to give our insights. We must be diligent to stay faithful to the Holy Spirit’s intended meaning. We strive to “stay on the line” of Scripture , never going above it by adding to it (which can result in undue speculation or legalism) or going below it by taking away from it (avoiding unpleasant or confusing passages, or altering the meaning to what we want it to mean). Second, the Bible is one big story, with one Hero of the story (Luke 24:27). From Genesis to Revelation—creation, fall, redemption, and restoration—we see God at work to reconcile people to himself. The Old Testament points to our need for and anticipation of a Savior, and the New Testament records and reflects on that Savior. Understanding this one big story helps reveal the significance of each passage. Third, context is king and questions are key . Context is the setting in which something occurs, and it always guides our interpretation. We consider both the literary context (what comes before and after a passage) and the historical context (the situation in which the original audience found themselves). To “stay on the line,” asking in-depth questions of the passage is vital, so we introduced the participants to questions for an epistle . In small-group time, we had each woman read the group’s assigned passage aloud because a thoughtful reading aids understanding, as does hearing the passage multiple times. 圣经研究是许多教会中妇女各部的心跳。 越来越多的教会更喜欢现场教学, 这可能会给妇女部主任带来挑战: 我们在哪里找到老师? 圣经老师不会来。 我们必须通过训练培养他们。

无论妇女以前或现在都从未教授过《圣经》,我们都能通过认真的教导和实践,帮助她们成长并获得“正确处理真相”的信心(2 Tim.2:15)。 为了让教会里的女人能够教书, 我帮助开发了一个四会的课程。 以下是我们如何发展和实施这种培训。

Get Organization I首先招募了两位有教授"圣经"经验的女性,我们一起通过上线的"西门信托第一妇女原则"课程,准备成为教官. 然后,我们将我们学到的原则个性化,以适应我们为教会中其他妇女的培训目标。

由于有不同的策略 接近各种流派的经典, 我们第一次举办这个课程, 我们选择培训妇女 如何教授一个故事。 我们挑选了一名彼得作为我们的案文,并指派每个小组在全程中工作一段。 例如,第1组有1个Peter 1:1–12,第2组有1:13–21,第3组有4:12–19.

我们用5:1–11作为我们作为一个整体研究的共同段落. 在随后的课程中,我们选择了其他的"圣经"流派:用福音书的段落进行叙事,而用诗作"智慧"/"诗". 圣经老师不会来。 我们必须通过训练培养他们。

我们以明确的目的促进了培训:帮助参与者提高理解和教授上帝之道的能力。 我们阐述了我们的期望:出席所有四场会议,完成作业,向同行传授十分钟的信息。 对培训的个别关注是关键所在,因此,我们指派每个参与者到一个由3至6名妇女组成的小组,并有一名领导人。

我们努力“坚持”《圣经》,决不通过增加《圣经》而超越《圣经》(这可能导致不适当的猜测或法律主义),或通过取走《圣经》而低于《圣经》(避免令人不快或令人困惑的段落,或改变《圣经》的含义)。 第二,"圣经"是一个大故事,有一个故事的英雄(公爵24:27).

从创世纪到启示——创造、倒下、赎回、复原——我们看见上帝在努力使人民与自己和解。 "旧约"指出我们对救世主的需求和期待,"新约"记载并反思了"救世主". 了解这个大故事有助于揭示每个段落的意义. 第三,背景是国王,问题是关键。

title: When Morningness Is Confused with Godliness
summary: Could it be possible that our idealizing of morning quiet times is more cultural than biblical?
summary_zh: 我们对早晨安静时间的理想化是否比圣经更具文化性？
title_zh: 当早晨与虔诚混淆时
content: “Do your quiet time with God every morning.” “Give God your first hours (your best hours!) of the day.” “Rise early for Scripture and prayer; it sets the tone for the rest of your day!” From pulpits to podcasts, I’ve heard these sentiments often in Christian circles. The instructions aren’t just to spend alone time with God but to specifically do so as the very first act of your day. For many, the “morning quiet time” has become a measuring rod of how well you’re doing in your relationship with God. Actor Mark Wahlberg once went viral on Instagram for a screenshot of his morning routine : waking up at 2:30 a.m., praying at 2:45, and completing his first workout before 5:30. This is one of many examples of how early rising has become associated with aspirational godliness. But is it really more virtuous to be a morning person than a night owl? What If You Have to Sleep In? Behind the modern mindset of hyperidealized mornings is the assumption that being a “morning person” is a virtue in and of itself—a gritty choice toward wellness and productivity within everyone’s power. The implication is that if you’re disciplined and wise, you’ll set the alarm clock and start the day early; you’ll make it happen. If you’re slothful or foolish, you won’t. Extenuating circumstances are just excuses. For many, the ‘morning quiet time’ has become a measuring rod of how well you’re doing in your relationship with God. But what would this mean for nurses whose work begins and ends when it’s dark outside? What about parents with newborns, whose babies’ demands don’t abide by our ideal rhythms? How about Christians who are naturally night owls: most alert, focused, and productive at night? Should these folks just suck it up and aspire to get up earlier in spite of their circumstances? Or could it be possible that our idealizing of morning quiet times is more cultural than biblical? God Loves Early Risers At first glance, it might seem that God’s Word does value our mornings most. Pastor David Mathis wrote an insightful article summarizing the abundance of instances in Scripture in which God’s people (including Christ himself!) either rose early to good effect or were directed by God to do so. Consider the Psalms: In Psalm 5:3, David says, “O LORD, in the morning you hear my voice.” In Psalm 88:13, the Sons of Korah sing, “In the morning my prayer comes before you.” In Psalm 90:14, Moses prays to God, “Satisfy us in the morning with your steadfast love, that we may rejoice and be glad all our days.” God clearly meets with his people in the morning. Case closed? Not quite. When you consult the whole counsel of Scripture, it becomes clear that God emphasizes meditating on his Word, singing his praises, and praying to his name just as much in the night as in the morning. Nocturnal Worship Let’s explore some nighttime examples. In Acts 16:25–26, after Paul and Silas are imprisoned in Philippi, God’s Word notably mentions the timing of their worship: “About midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God . . .” Silas and Paul don’t try to go to sleep early so they can engage with God at the crack of dawn. They stay up late, worshiping at midnight. The results are profound. In Psalm 63:5–6, David prays to the Lord, “My soul will be satisfied as with fat and rich food, and my mouth will praise you with joyful lips, when I remember you upon my bed, and meditate on you in the watches of the night.” This psalm as a whole is arguably a nighttime prayer. David prays these lyrics to the Lord seemingly all while on his “bed,” singing midnight praises. Consider Jesus’s earthly life. On the fateful day before his crucifixion, when it comes to spending devoted time alone with his Father, Jesus prays passionately, in Gethsemane, at night (Matt. 26:36–56). There is no mention in the Gospels of Jesus rising early on this momentous day; it might have happened, but the recorded emphasis is Jesus’s spiritual devotion in the dark. Morning and evening aren’t

title: Contend Without Being Contentious
summary: In an age marked by theological compromise and unnecessary outrage, we need church leaders who can do more than win arguments.
summary_zh: 在一个以神学妥协和不必要的愤怒为标志的时代，我们需要教会领袖，他们能做的不仅仅是赢得争论。
title_zh: 在不引起争议的情况下进行竞争
content: “How do we contend for the faith biblically without becoming quarrelsome and contentious?” A member of my (Barry’s) congregation posed this thoughtful yet difficult question when our church was studying the letter of Jude. In his purpose statement (vv. 3–4), Jude says he wants to write about the salvation he shares in common with his recipients. However, he finds it necessary instead to exhort them to “contend for the faith.” What does obeying this exhortation involve? Before we contend for the faith, it’s essential to clarify how to approach confrontation and why we’re seeking to confront in the first place. Knowing myself, I (Ben) can have many sinful and unhelpful reasons for confronting; my pride often tempts me to seek my glory in confrontation rather than seeking the Lord’s glory. Yet when our motivation is wrong, our manner is too. Then, contending can quickly become contentiousness. Jude gives us a better way. Why and How To Confront His letter provides a framework for Christians to discern when we should confront error, and with what level of intensity. Jude provides four basic confrontation categories that will help us defend the truth without becoming quarrelsome. 1. Oppose deceivers (v. 4). We must be able to distinguish between those who are confused and those who are deceivers. Not everyone who errs is a malicious false teacher. Some simply need patient guidance, instruction, and compassionate discipleship. Jude’s letter provides a framework for Christians to discern when we should confront error, and with what level of intensity. But others actively promote error, refuse to submit to biblical authority, or sow seeds of division that can lead God’s people away from Christ. Jude has deceivers in mind as his primary concern in his letter. He’s concerned not just that they’re in error but that they’re influential. For that reason, he wants the church to have the Spirit-led courage to confront the deceivers’ errors. Such contending requires wisdom. For pastors, it can involve correcting false teaching both privately and publicly. You may need to warn your church about dangerous influences or refuse to give a platform to those who persistently distort the gospel. Remember, Paul instructs elders to rebuke those who contradict sound doctrine (Titus 1:9) and to protect God’s flock from spiritual wolves (Acts 20:28–31). He also warns congregations to watch out for divisive teachers (Rom. 16:17–18). When we confront deceivers, our aim isn’t to embarrass them or to win arguments. Rather, we contend for the faith because truth matters and because Christ’s church matters. 2. Instruct doubters (v. 22). In the Christian life, we encounter many who have doubts about the faith. They know the truth, but they struggle to believe it. Instructing those who doubt may not seem like contending for the faith at first, but gently clearing up their concerns strengthens both their faith and the church’s faith. Contending well for doubters can prevent them from wandering or even from becoming deceivers. It’s an act of mercy (v. 22), and it must be done mercifully. When believers doubt or begin to waver on the truth, our responsibility isn’t to ruthlessly force truth on them. We also shouldn’t ignore their questions. Neither response is merciful. Instead, we must engage doubters’ questions with compassion, trusting that the Lord will reveal truth to them in his time. Our belief in Scripture’s sufficiency is critical here. God’s Word, not our teaching or apologetic skill, possesses the power to reveal his truth. Doubts are many and various, but the Bible remains constant and trustworthy. 3. Warn wanderers (v. 23). Between doubting and deceiving stands another category: wandering. Some in the church drift, or have drifted, toward dangerous doctrinal error or patterns of sin that, if left unchecked, will lead to their fall. Jude prescribes the appropriate response: “Save others by snatching them out of the fire” (v. 23). His imagery conveys urge

title: Editor’s Pick: New Children’s Picture Books
summary: Let these stories remind you to enjoy the goodness of the moment and, even as it changes to something new, that God’s goodness is everlasting.
summary_zh: 让这些故事提醒你享受当下的美好，即使它变成了新的东西，神的美好是永恒的。
title_zh: 编辑精选：全新儿童图画书
content: Autumn is a season of changes. At our home, as the leaves yellowed and the days shortened, my youngest child started middle school. That means picture books have me feeling a little nostalgia for the past these days, right alongside a lot of excitement for new things to come. Many of these books are about big changes and adjusting to them, like living with a new baby, moving to a new place, or finding a new heart in Christ’s kingdom. But some are also about the little changes happening around us every day, like laughter over a fleeting moment of childhood imagination or settling down to sleep to prepare for a new day. With all these experiences arriving on the horizon and then flying past like interstate billboards, it’s sweet to remember that “every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom there is no variation or shadow due to change” (James 1:17). As you hand one of these brand-new books to a young reader or curl up to enjoy it together, let these stories remind you to enjoy the goodness of the moment, even as it is changing to something new, and that God’s goodness is everlasting. 1. God Gives Sleep by Betsy Childs Howard, illustrated by Bethan Welby ( TGC Store | Amazon) When our family was exhausted and planning a big move with four children ages 6 and under, I really could have used this little book from Betsy Childs Howard. God Gives Sleep is a rhyming board book with illustrations of adorable animals (sleeping ladybugs!) and two simple refrains that even very young listeners can repeat or “read” for themselves: “God gives sleep” and “God will keep.” Both reflect promises from God that feel vital to the early days of parenting filled with sweet, sleepy snuggles and long, sleepless nights. The last picture shows the entire family asleep and includes Isaiah 40:31 (“Those who hope in the LORD will renew their strength,” NIV). God Gives Sleep is engaging, gentle, funny, and wise, and I’ve already given it to parents of new babies. 2. Winnie-the-Pooh: The Graphic Novel by A. A. Milne, adapted by Kevan Chandler and Joe Sutphin ( Amazon ) Full disclosure: I’m a huge Pooh fan. I’ve probably read the original Milne book dozens of times, and I can be a little sniffy about adaptations. But I loved this one. While I missed Milne’s distinctive narration in parts of the storytelling, this graphic novel retains enough of the original language and has such beautiful artwork that it easily justifies its existence. Parents of young independent readers often ask me for recommendations for books complex enough to be engaging but with content and formatting suitable for early elementary school. This version perfectly fits that space where 6-to-9-year-olds can track the story through the pictures but also enjoy the challenge of some complex vocabulary (“Sudden and Temporary Immersion”) and jokes that reward context research (“An ambush is a sort of Surprise.” “So is a gorse-bush sometimes.”). Winnie-the-Pooh: The Graphic Novel is a sweet and worthy tribute to this classic celebration of early childhood in all its imaginative wonder. 3. The Upside-Down, Inside-Out, Can’t-Believe-It Kingdom by Jonathan Landry Cruse, illustrated by Joe Hox ( Amazon ) The adventure begins with a son begging his father to tell him an exciting bedtime story with dragons and knights. The result is this retelling of the gospel as a quest with a king and a prince and a reminder of our humble place in the kingdom. Joe Hox’s illustrations stand out for being traditional and bright, with a dragon that isn’t too fierce for younger readers but also enough detail within the pictures to engage older readers. The story tells us that the good King will “make us be strong with the strength of His might,” a powerful message for young knights who want to do great things for the kingdom. 4. Doing Something New: A Prayer for Beginnings by Mitali Perkins, illustrated by Andrés Landazábal ( Amazon ) Mitali Perkins includes a n
content_zh:
秋为一季之变. 在家中,随着叶子被黄了,日子被缩短,我最小的孩子开始上中学. 这意味着图书让我觉得过去有些怀旧, 与很多刺激 来的新事物。

这些书中很多是关于大变化并适应它们,比如与新婴儿一起生活,搬到新地方,或者在基督的王国中找到新的心. 但有些人也谈到我们周围每天发生的小变化,比如在童年短暂的想象中欢笑,或者沉睡以准备新的一天。

随着所有这些经历的到来,然后像州际告示牌一样飞过,令人欣慰的是,“每一个好的礼物和完美的礼物都是来自上面,来自灯之父,与他一起没有变化或阴影。” (詹姆斯1:17)。

当你把这些全新的书交给一个年轻的读者 或整理起来一起欣赏的时候, 让这些故事提醒你享受这一刻的美好, 即使它正在变成新的事物, 上帝的善良是永恒的。 1. 联合国

由Bethan Welby(TGC Store QQ Amazon)所展示, 当家庭精疲力竭,计划一个大动作 四个孩子6岁和6岁以下, 我真的可以用这本小书 从贝茜 Childs Howard。

上帝赐予睡眠(God Gives Sleep)是一本配有可爱动物(sleeping ladybugs!)插图的韵律板书,还有两个简单的节奏,即使非常年轻的听众也能为自己重复或“阅读 ” : “ 上帝赐予睡眠 ” 和“上帝会保留 ” 。 两者都反映了上帝的诺言,这些诺言对养育孩子的早期至关重要,充满了甜蜜的,沉睡的和漫长的,无眠的夜晚.

最后一张图片显示整个家庭都睡了,包括以赛亚40:31(“那些希望被耶和华唤起力量的人”,NIV)。 上帝赐予睡眠的热情、温和、幽默和智慧, 由Kevan Chandler和Joe Sutphin(亚马逊)改编 全面披露:我是一个巨大的维尼粉丝。

我可能读过Milne的原作数十次, 但我爱这个 虽然我错过了Milne在故事部分的突出叙事,

年轻独立读者的家长经常向我征求关于书本复杂到足以参与,但内容和格式适合初等学校的建议。

这一版本完全适合6至9岁的人通过图片追踪故事的空间,但也享受一些复杂词汇的挑战(“突然和暂时的印象”)和奖励上下文研究的笑话(“埋伏是一种惊喜”)。 “有时粗鲁也是。 ”

Winnie-the-Pooh:"图形小说"(The Graphic Newvel)是对这一经典的幼儿期庆祝活动的甜美而值得称道的赞誉,在其所有富有想象力的奇迹中. 3. 乔纳森·兰德里·克鲁斯(Jonathan Landry Cruse)的《上下、内出、不能相信的王国》。 冒险从一个乞求父亲的儿子开始,告诉他一个令人兴奋的与龙和骑士同床共枕的故事.

结果是福音的重现 与国王和王子一起探索 并提醒我们在王国的卑微地位 乔·霍克斯的插画突出表现为传统和明亮, 龙对年轻读者来说不是太凶猛,

故事告诉我们,好国王将“以他的力量使我们强大起来”,这是希望为王国做大事的年轻骑士的有力信息。 Mitali Perkins的《为开端祈祷》, Andrés Landazábal(亚马逊) 所描述,

title: How Memorizing the Sermon on the Mount Reorders My Heart
summary: In a world where algorithms capture our affections and lure us online via our cravings, one of the most effective resistance strategies we can employ is to study and memorize Scripture—especially the Sermon on the Mount.
summary_zh: 在一个算法捕捉我们的感情并通过我们的渴望在网上引诱我们的世界里，我们可以使用的最有效的抵抗策略之一是学习和背诵圣经，尤其是登山宝训。
title_zh: 背诵登山宝训如何重塑我的心
content: A couple of years ago, two college students challenged me—a woman in her 50s—to memorize the Sermon on the Mount (Matt. 5–7). Inwardly, I balked, but now I know that few things in my 35 years of following Jesus have been more transformative than committing Jesus’s most famous sermon to memory. John Stott wrote that the Sermon on the Mount is “the nearest thing to a manifesto that [Jesus] ever uttered, for it is his own description of what he wanted his followers to be and to do.” After spending the last few years memorizing it, I see with increasing clarity that I need Jesus’s help to live out what he taught. In a world where algorithms capture our affections and lure us online via our cravings, one of the most effective resistance strategies we can employ is to study and memorize Scripture—especially the Sermon on the Mount. Create a New Algorithm The algorithm often knows us better than we know ourselves. Every time we buy something on Amazon or pause to watch a reel on social media, the algorithm chronicles our activities and builds a profile of us. This profile shows our real interests (not just the ones we list in our social media bios) and some of our most private behaviors (the ones we thank God aren’t live streamed). In milliseconds, companies use what the algorithm knows about us to discover the most effective way to get us to buy their products. In the same way that the algorithm learns about us with each post we like and each reel we watch, God’s Word comes alive in us with every command we learn and put into practice, with every verse we ponder, and with every teaching we adopt as a way of life. By absorbing and obeying Jesus’s Sermon on the Mount, we can create a feedback loop that enlarges his kingdom rule over our lives. Let Scripture Reorder Your Heart Before I started my memorization project, I’d heard many Christians tout Scripture memory as one of the most potent tools for conforming to Jesus, but I didn’t take it seriously. All that changed when I realized algorithms had more access to my life than God’s Word did. By absorbing and obeying Jesus’s Sermon on the Mount, we can create a feedback loop that enlarges his kingdom rule over our lives. Like many Americans, I was averaging more than two hours daily scrolling social media and shopping online, and much less time reading the Bible. I’d thought lack of time was my biggest obstacle to memorizing Scripture. But in reality, my affections and priorities were the obstacle. Memorizing and studying the Sermon on the Mount has provided a powerful reset. I’ve noticed two significant changes in my life. 1. My thoughts are increasingly populated by Jesus’s desires for me. Previously, I was easily shaped by what internet influencers said I should be doing and what my heart really wanted to do. Now, Scripture tenderly draws me to Christ’s transforming grace. For example, a few months ago, someone wrote harsh words to me. I couldn’t sidestep what I’d memorized: Pray for those who hurt you (Mt. 5:44) In those difficult interactions, Jesus’s teaching gave me wisdom to stop reacting and start praying for the one lashing out. Pausing to pray breaks down my self-protective stance so I can consider what the log in my eye might be (Mt. 7:5). 2. I see how vastly different God’s kingdom is from the world we live in. I no longer feel as drawn to the shallow version of perfection the algorithm offers me—the beautiful home, the perfectly fit woman charmingly dressed, or the promise of perpetual travel. When I stop to linger over another picture-perfect kitchen, the Sermon on the Mount prompts me to consider where my treasure really is. These chapters have given me a robust lens through which I can view all of God’s Word. After drinking so deeply of Jesus’s sermon , I see it as the hinge on which both the Old Testament and the New Testament hang. I had thought lack of time was my biggest obstacle to memorizing Scripture. But in reality, my affections and priorities were the obstacl
content_zh:
几年前,两个大学生挑战我——一个50多岁的女性——要记住山上赛门(Matt. 5-7). 但现在我知道,在我追随耶稣的35年里, 没有什么事情比把耶稣最出名的布道当作记忆更具有变革性。

约翰·斯托特(John Stott)写道:"山上赛蒙是[耶稣]曾经发表的宣言中最接近的东西,因为这是他自己对追随者所希望的和所要做的事的描述". 我越来越清楚地看到,我需要耶稣的帮助来维持他所教的。

在一个算法捕捉到我们感情并通过我们的渴望来引诱我们上线的世界中,我们可以采用的最有效的抵抗策略之一是学习并记住"圣经"——特别是"山上"的"塞尔门". 创建新算法 算法常常比我们自己更了解我们.

每次我们购买亚马逊或暂停观看社交媒体的片段, 算法记录我们的活动, 以及一些最私人的行为(我们感谢上帝的人不是活生生的)。

在毫秒内,公司利用算法了解我们的情况,发现最有效的方法让我们购买他们的产品. 正如算法用我们所喜欢的每一个帖子和我们所看的每一卷片子来了解我们一样,上帝的言语以我们所学习和运用的每一个命令、我们所思考的每一个诗句和我们所采纳的作为生活方式的每一个教义,在我们中充满活力。

通过吸收和服从耶稣在"山上"的赛蒙,我们可以建立一个反馈回路,扩大他的王国对我们生活的统治. 在开始我的回忆计划之前, 我听到许多基督徒将圣经记忆说成是符合耶稣的最有力工具之一,

当我意识到算法与上帝的言语相比, 通过吸收和服从耶稣在"山上"的赛蒙,我们可以建立一个反馈回路,扩大他的王国对我们生活的统治. 我和许多美国人一样,平均每天有两个多小时 滚动社交媒体和网上购物, 阅读圣经的时间要少得多。

我本以为没有时间是我记起圣经的最大障碍。 但实际上,我的爱和优先考虑是障碍。 纪念并研究了"山上"的"塞尔门"提供了强大的重置. 我注意到我生命中有两个重大的变化。 1. 耶稣对我的渴望使我的思想日益丰富。

之前,我很容易被网络影响者 说我应该做什么 和我的心真正想要做什么。 现在,《圣经》轻而易举地吸引我走向基督的恩典。 例如,几个月前,有人给我写了严厉的话. 我无法回避我所记住的:为伤害你的人祈祷(Mt.

5:44 在困难的交往中,耶稣的教导给了我智慧,让我停止反应,开始为那一次狂欢祈祷. 暂停祈祷 打破自我保护的姿势 这样我就可以考虑我的眼中可能是什么(7:5山) 2. 我看到上帝的王国与我们生活的世界大相径庭。

我不再觉得算法能吸引到我的 浅薄的完美版本, 当我停止停留 停留在另一个图片完美的厨房, 山上赛门 促使我考虑 我的宝藏到底在哪里。

这些章节给了我一个强烈的透镜,我可以透视上帝的所有言语。 在饮用耶稣的布道之后,我认为这是旧约和新约所依赖的。 我以为没有时间 是我记起圣经的最大障碍 但实际上,我的爱和优先 是迷信

title: Who Is the God of the Bible?
summary: Contemplating God’s names provides a deeper understanding of his being and attributes and a firmer foundation for our faith and hope.
summary_zh: 沉思神的名字可以更深入地了解祂的存在和属性，并为我们的信心和希望奠定更坚实的基础。
title_zh: 谁是圣经中的神？
content: According to the Belgic Confession , God reveals himself to us in two “books”: the book of nature (God’s world) and the book of Scripture (God’s written Word). The primary way God reveals himself in the book of Scripture is by proclaiming his name. In this first of two paired lectures from TGC25, Scott Swain considers several of the names whereby God reveals himself in the Bible. Contemplating God’s names provides a deeper understanding of his being and attributes and a firmer foundation for our faith and hope. It also helps us better appreciate the ways God reveals himself to us in Jesus Christ. title: ‘I Play Rocky’ Finds New Inspiration in an Old Story
summary: ‘I Play Rocky’ is the latest pop-culture celebration of storytelling as agency: telling your story in just the way you want it to be told.
summary_zh: “I Play Rocky”是将讲故事作为代理的最新流行文化庆祝活动：以您希望的方式讲述您的故事。
title_zh: 《我扮演洛基》在古老的故事中寻找新的灵感
content: Rocky debuted in theaters 50 years ago, in 1976—a bicentennial-year release that underscored the movie’s profound American spirit. Immediately a blockbuster and critical darling (the highest-grossing movie of 1976 and winner of the Best Picture Oscar), it has since become a pantheon film in American cinema. Rocky ’s Philadelphia setting and underdog, rags-to-riches story captured a hardscrabble American optimism, something that gave needed inspiration in the mid-1970s and resonates still today. Now in 2026—America’s semiquincentennial— Rocky is getting a theatrical rerelease. And a new movie, I Play Rocky (out today in select theaters) is telling the story of the iconic movie’s development, which is an underdog epic of its own. The movie, directed by Peter Farrelly ( Green Book ) and starring Anthony Ippolito in a breakout turn as Sylvester Stallone, is a refreshingly feel-good crowd pleaser. It’s the sort of well-made, intelligent, but also inspiring movie for grown-ups that feels like a dying breed in Hollywood. Movies About Moviemaking I Play Rocky (rated PG-13 for language) follows a well-worn template of a movie about the making of a classic movie. Saving Mr. Banks (2013) was about Walt Disney and the making of Mary Poppins . Hitchcock (2012) was about Alfred Hitchcock and the making of Psycho . Last year’s Nouvelle Vague was about Jean-Luc Godard and the making of Breathless . I Play Rocky is about Stallone and the making of Rocky . Hollywood loves making movies about itself: stories about storytelling, movies about moviemaking, actors playing actors. Hollywood loves making movies about itself: stories about storytelling, movies about moviemaking, actors playing actors. Self-reflexive inspiration goes back more than a century in cinema, perhaps starting with Dziga Vertov’s Man with a Movie Camera (1929). The 1950s produced classics like Sunset Boulevard (1950) and Singin’ in the Rain (1952), but the trend really picked up in the postmodern era in the 1960s and beyond: 8 ½ (1963), Day for Night (1973), Mulholland Drive (2001), Adaptation (2002), The Artist (2011), and Once Upon a Time . . . in Hollywood (2019). The list is long. A hallmark of postmodernity is a metaposture of knowing awareness—storytellers who know they’re storytellers and want the audience to know that they know. As postmodernism has given way to metamodernism , the trend of “movies about moviemaking” has continued, but in a slightly different register. These sorts of films are no longer merely metaexercises in self-awareness. The cerebral, cynical detachment of “films about filmmaking” like Barton Fink (1991), Ed Wood (1994), or even Who Framed Roger Rabbit (1988) has given way to metamodern expressions that blend cynicism and sincerity, self-awareness with earnest escapism. Steven Spielberg’s The Fabelmans (2022) is a recent example of a movie in this vein, and I Play Rocky has a similar feel. Even as it lifts the veil on the Hollywood myth factory and mines many laughs out of the fundamentally profit-seeking, money-centric nature of the movie business, it’s full of heart and soul. It has a joyful, hopeful, sincere, perhaps idealistic spirit (“I’d rather be an optimist and be wrong, than a pessimist and be right,” one character says). Refreshing Celebration of Marriage I also like how I Play Rocky celebrates the empowering beauty of marriage. The film opens with Stallone as a broke actor in New York, sometimes sleeping on the streets and at one point accepting a role in an X-rated adult film just to earn some desperately needed money (a dark part of Stallone’s past that the film plays for awkward laughs). He’s a lost soul with bleak prospects. But then he meets Sasha (AnnaSophia Robb), with whom he works at a movie theater. They get married and move to Los Angeles, and things start to turn around for him. As a husband and soon a father, Stallone feels more urgency to provide. He valets at a swanky Hollywood restaurant to pay the bills while he churns o

Rocky的费城设置和衰落, 从富人到富人的故事中抓住了美国令人费解的乐观, 现在在2026年——美国半个世纪. 洛基要重新上演戏剧

Hitchcock (2012) 是关于Alfred Hitchcock和制作"心理"的. 去年的Nouvelle Vague是关于让-吕克·戈达德(Jean-Luc Godard)和制造"无心"(Breathless)的。 我演奏"洛基"是为了斯达隆和制作"洛基" 好莱坞喜欢拍摄关于自己的电影:讲述故事的故事,关于电影制作的电影,演员扮演演员.

好莱坞喜欢拍摄关于自己的电影:讲述故事的故事,关于电影制作的电影,演员扮演演员. 在电影院里,自我反省灵感可以追溯到一个多世纪,也许从Dziga Vertov用电影相机的人(1929年)开始.

20世纪50年代出品了"日落大道"(1950年)和"雨中之星"(1952年)等经典作品,但1960年代及以后的后现代时代,这一趋势确实有所回升:8⁄2(1963年),"为晚"(1973年),"穆尔霍克兰"(Mulholland Drive)(2001),"适应"(2002年),"艺术家"(2011年)和"Once Upon a Time"(2019年). 名单很长。

后现代的标志是认识认识的变相, 后现代主义已经让位于现代主义, 这些类型的电影不再仅仅是自我意识中的元活.

巴顿·芬克(1991年)、埃德·伍德(1994年)等“关于电影制作的电影”、甚至《谁陷害了罗杰·兔子》(1988年)的狂热、愤世嫉俗的散漫,让位给现代的表达方式,这些表达方式将愤世嫉俗和真诚、自我意识与真诚的自负相融合。 史蒂文·斯皮尔伯格所著"法贝尔曼斯"(2022年)是此脉中一部电影的一出近代例子,而"我扮演洛基"也有类似的感觉.

即使它揭开好莱坞神话工厂的面纱, 我更喜欢乐观与错误,

title: How the Lord’s Supper Fuels Spiritual Growth
summary: Calvin shows us that the Lord’s Supper is fuel for spiritual growth, so we should come to the table expectantly every time.
summary_zh: 加尔文向我们表明，主的晚餐是灵性成长的燃料，所以我们每次都应该期待地来到餐桌前。
title_zh: 主的晚餐如何促进灵性成长
content: Recently, I (and my peers) have experienced a number of parishioners converting to Catholicism. As I’ve talked to these converts, they’ve consistently brought up the Lord’s Table. They find encouragement in identifying the bread and wine with Jesus’s body and blood. I’ve heard statements such as this: Pastor George, I like the idea that Jesus was talking about the Lord’s supper when he said, “Whoever feeds on my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him” (John 6:56). My faith just feels more real if I’m literally bringing Jesus into my body on a daily basis. While this phenomenon seems to be happening with greater frequency, it’s not totally new. Years ago, I served alongside a man at an ordination service for another pastor in our city. I hadn’t met this man before; I only knew he had until recently been a professor at a Reformed and evangelical seminary. This man preached a solid message on Jesus’s call for ministers of the gospel, and I thanked him for it. Then, the next day, I saw him being interviewed on TV. I tuned in just as he explained, I needed more realism than my tradition provided, so during lunch I would walk down to the local Roman Catholic parish and take the Eucharist. To unite literally with Jesus’s body and blood was more deeply satisfying to me than the “mystery of union with Christ” my church taught. So, I resigned my post at the seminary and went home to Rome. I could relate other conversations with those who have left the Reformed faith and joined the Roman Catholic, Orthodox, or Anglo-Catholic traditions. A similar theme runs through them all: the desire for a more transformational, sensory reality than what the Reformed view of the Lord’s supper provides. Is this critique valid? How would John Calvin respond to the critique that if you follow the Reformed view of the supper, you’re missing out on its power? Transformed at the Table Sometimes, in an effort to have biblically faithful theology, Reformed Christians speak only of what the communion elements are not . I’m painfully aware of my of shortcomings in this regard. This can inadvertently drive some believers to seek out a more “real” experience in other traditions. We can get caught up in debating the exact nature of the bread and wine and forget to ask the more pressing question: How should this meal change me today? Let’s look back at Calvin’s teachings on communion. When we do, we’ll recover a renewed vision for the table, one that sees it as a divine encounter that motivates a transformed life of profound gratitude and obedience. In short, Calvin shows us that the Lord’s supper is fuel for spiritual growth, so we should come to the table expectantly every time. In Calvin’s “ Short Treatise on the Lord’s Supper ,” he writes that the supper fuels the believer’s spiritual growth in at least three ways. 1. The supper assures us of our inheritance in Christ. Calvin teaches that Jesus uses his table to assure us of our inheritance. He doesn’t merely mean that the supper gives us a psychological boost. He means that assurance comes by means of a real union between Christ and the believer, and he means that our experience of this union is expedited by faithfully partaking in the covenant meal. Calvin shows us that the Lord’s supper is fuel for spiritual growth, so we should come to the table expectantly every time. In his commentary on Ephesians, Calvin writes , “Paul says that we are members of his [Christ’s] flesh and of his bones. Do we wonder then, that in the Lord’s Supper he holds out his body to be enjoyed by us, and to nourish us unto eternal life?” Calvin insists that by faith, Christians are made members of Jesus’s fleshly human body, so at communion, we experience all the benefits of spiritual union with him. Christ took on flesh so that in his ascended state, he might be a channel of righteousness to the believer, pouring into him all that Christ’s human life accomplished. title: To Sustain Inner-City Church Plants, Adopt a Missionary Model
summary: To plant churches in these spaces, we need to think like missionaries.
summary_zh: 要在这些地方建造教堂，我们需要像传教士一样思考。
title_zh: 为了维持内城教会植物，采用传教士模式
content: In a conversation at church one Sunday, a pastor told a friend of mine, “Your friend should quit trying to plant churches in the inner city. It doesn’t happen because it can’t happen.” I was visiting this friend just before COVID-19 hit, speaking at a separate church about our ministry, New England Urban Church Planting. Our organization was new, and my sinful inclination was to think, Oh, you just wait and see! My friend was equally defensive. Yet this pastor was onto something: It rarely happens, and it is indeed hard. Why is church planting in our nation’s neglected inner cities so rare? Why are underserved urban communities overlooked by gospel-preaching churches? Stakeholders in our ministry have discussed these questions since 2009, leading to the organization’s founding in 2020. We’ve learned a lot in these years of full-time work as we’re growing this network of inner-city planters. The work is hard for two key reasons. Yet it’s possible. And it’s crucial. Christ has commanded us to make disciples of all nations (Matt. 28:19)—this includes in our own nation’s inner cities. To plant churches in these spaces, we need to think like missionaries. Problem Unless you grew up in the inner city, serving there is a cross-cultural experience. This is the first reason church planting hard. Ruby Payne asks her readers if they can survive in poverty: Do you know how to keep your clothes from being stolen from a laundromat? Do you know how to move in half a day? Do you know how to keep your car from getting repossessed if you fall behind on payments? Discipling men and women in the inner city can be exasperating when they have a new burner phone frequently. Inner-city pastors need to know how to preach and how to administer Narcan. And behind all that is the sound of gunshots, fights, loud TVs, and the quiet exit of well-meaning suburban Christians who came to help but didn’t last long. Christ has commanded us to make disciples of all nations—this includes in our own nation’s inner cities. Evangelicalism often feels like it’s married to only one culture: suburbia. Postwar Americans migrated from our cities to set up homes and churches in the suburbs. In 1940, 15 percent of Americans lived in the suburbs. By 2000, that number was 50 percent. Evangelicals were a disproportionately high percentage of those who made the move. As this happened, Brian Miller argues , the values of suburbia melded with and shaped the values of evangelicalism. Churches in impoverished neighborhoods are rarely financially self-sustaining—the second challenge. Even if a pastor disciples his church toward generosity, being generous with a poverty-level income won’t pay the bills. So pastors who serve in these places get beaten down by serving a needy congregation while holding two other jobs “on the side.” It’s unsustainable. We don’t believe the answer for inner-city pastors should be a bi- or trivocational life. Solution The solution to these two challenges is within reach: the model of a supported foreign missionary. Since the late 18th century, the church has been training and sustaining men and women for gospel work in unfamiliar places, where they cannot expect the financial support of locals. This training-and-supporting model should be applied to inner-city church planting. The change we need has four aspects. The first is a change of heart. We need gospel-saturated hearts that understand that all people are impoverished by sin. Those living in a homeless encampment share the same fundamental condition as the wealthy suburbanite. Filled with gospel grace, we can move toward the poor because we’re more alike at heart than we are different. Our hearts must be shaped by the reality of Christ’s initiative to leave the riches of heaven for us, to become poor for us, that we might become rich (2 Cor. 8:9). Second, we need to believe that God’s heart is particularly inclined toward the overlooked (Ps. 72:12–14) and toward those generous toward them (Prov. 14:

title: Report Cards on Your Actions Won’t Fix Your Heart
summary: From GLP-1s to political reposts to mindfulness streaks, we’re all keeping score. Jesus says you can’t know who you are until you look at your heart.
summary_zh: 从GLP-1到政治转发，再到正念条纹，我们都在记分。耶稣说，除非你看看自己的内心，否则你无法知道自己是谁。
title_zh: 关于您行动的报告卡片无法修复您的心脏
content: Who am I? All cultures, human philosophies, and religious systems try to answer this question in a way that leads to a meaningful life. We want to find in them a path that allows us to say, “Who am I? I’m a good person. I’m someone who is living a good and right life.” What paths toward goodness and righteousness are being offered today? They’re as vast and varied as ever. One popular path is to optimize your life via medical improvements, ranging from plastic surgery to GLP-1s. The more you can “ humanmaxx ” your body to look healthier and be stronger, the more likely you’ll be considered an ideal human being—a good person to hire, to be friends with, to date or marry. Political engagement is another common path. Your goodness is determined by how connected you are to particular political movements. You can feel like you’re a good person when you make sure you quickly like and repost all Zohran Mamdani’s videos. Or alternatively, you’ll be affirmed as a good person by how aggressively you go after or insult people who like Mamdani. Paths our culture offers to the good life are often combined. Your sense of how good a person you are is measured by a mixture of how long you’ve engaged in therapy, how many hours you volunteer at your children’s school, and how long your streak is on your mindfulness app. Tara Isabella Burton, in her book Strange Rites: New Religions for a Godless World , argues that people have formed their own religious systems by drawing from various religions and philosophies. People have become “creators of their own bespoke religions, mixing and matching spiritual and aesthetic and experiential and philosophical traditions.” We’re doing a DIY project, grabbing and piecing together whatever’s around us, hoping we can come up with something to help us in our journey. So, what path does Christianity offer to assure us we’re living a good and righteous life? Keeping Score The Christian approach is to address what the Bible calls the heart. The heart is the Bible’s shorthand term for describing the part of you that drives and motivates you, what dictates your thoughts and emotions. Christianity starts with the heart because this is the only real way by which you can determine who you are and what needs to change. We see the contrast between the religious and cultural approach and the Christian approach in Jesus’s interaction with the Pharisees in Matthew 15:1–20. The Pharisees confront Jesus to ask him why his disciples don’t wash their hands before eating. Handwashing before meals was one of the many religious rules the Pharisees had developed, practiced, and called others to practice. For the Pharisees, the best answer to the question “Who am I?” was based on how well they followed their set standards. If a person kept the standard and had a life that could be observed to follow all the rules, then that person could definitively say to themselves and those around them, “I’m a good person who is living a good and right life.” Jesus’s story about the Pharisee in Luke 18:9–14 is another example. The Pharisee intently notes in his prayer how he, unlike the tax collector praying next to him, fasts twice a week and always gives the full tithe. Jesus describes the Pharisees in Matthew 6 as people who make sure their regular prayers can be seen and affirmed by all. The Pharisees weren’t alone in this approach. Greco-Roman religion had its own rules and standards to follow. Its gods demanded rituals, sacrifices, and festivals to appease and honor them. Performed rightly, they’d result in people securing the blessing they needed from the gods, thus assuring them their lives were good and righteous. Jesus, however, reframes the Pharisees’ questioning by showing that their approach doesn’t go far enough. Right living and human flourishing demands more than one’s outward actions. It requires harder interior examination. And that means looking at the heart. Jesus says, “What comes out of the mouth proceeds from the heart” (
content_zh:
我是谁? 所有文化,人类哲学,宗教体系都试图以导致有意义的生活的方式来回答这个问题. 我们想在他们中间找到一条道路,使我们能够说:“我是谁? 我是个好人。 我是一个过着良好和正确生活的人。 今天为善良和正义提供了哪些途径? 他们和以往一样,

一个通俗的途径是通过医疗改进来优化你的生活,从整形手术到GLP-1. 你越能"人类马克思"你的身体看起来越健康,越强壮,你就越有可能被认为是理想的人——一个能雇佣、成为朋友、约会或结婚的好人。 政治参与是另一条共同道路。

你的善良取决于你和特定政治运动的关系 也觉得自己是个好人, 或以你对马姆达尼的追求或侮辱来证明你是一个好人。 我们的文化为美好生活提供的道路常常是结合在一起的。

你对一个人有多好的感觉,是通过你从事治疗的时间、你在学校志愿工作多少小时、以及你的心智应用上多久来衡量的。

Tara Isabella Burton在她所著"陌生的Rites:新宗教为无神的世界"一书中认为,人们通过从各种宗教和哲学中汲取来形成自己的宗教体系.

人们已经成为“他们自己所讲的宗教的创造者,混合和配合精神和美学以及体验和哲学传统。” 我们正在进行一个DIY计划, 抓取和整理我们周围的东西, 希望我们能想出一些东西来帮助我们的旅程。 基督教给我们提供了什么途径来保证我们过着美好和正义的生活?

记分 基督教的方法是解决"圣经"所说的"心". 心灵是圣经的简称,用来描述你推动和激励你,决定你思想和情绪的部分。 基督教以心为起点,因为这是你决定自己是谁和需要改变的惟一真正方法.

在耶稣与法利赛人的互动中, 法利赛人面对耶稣, 餐前洗手是法利赛人制定,练习的众多宗教规则之一,并号召其他人去练习.

对法利赛人来说,“我是谁?” 问题的最佳答案在于他们遵守既定标准的情况。

如果一个人能遵守标准,并过着可以遵守所有规则的生活,那么这个人可以肯定地对自己和周围的人说,“我是个好人,正在过上良好和正确的生活。” 耶稣在卢克18:9–14中讲述了法利赛人的故事是另一个例子.

法利赛人在祷告中故意记下他如何与旁边的收税者不同的是,他每周斋戒两次并总是给满分之一. 耶稣在"马太福音"6中将法利赛人描述为确保他们的定期祷告能被所有人都看到和肯定的人. 法利赛人并不孤单。 格雷科-罗马宗教有自己的规则和标准可以遵循。

它的神要求举行仪式,祭祀,并举行节日来安抚和尊崇他们. 让他们得到神赐予的祝福, 但耶稣重新定义了法利赛人的质疑,

正确的生活和人类的繁荣需要不止一种外向行动。 这需要更严格的内部检查。 并谓观心相. 耶稣说,“从口中出出的东西从心脏中得来。”

title: Building a Workplace Where People Flourish (with Landon Hobson)
summary: What happens when a seminary-trained economist takes over a pet-products plant? Landon Hobson, CEO of Cosmos Corporation, shares how paid mission days, a book club, and a ‘make the coffee’ ethic help ordinary workers flourish.
summary_zh: 当受过神学院培训的经济学家接管宠物产品工厂时会发生什么？ Cosmos Corporation首席执行官兰登·霍布森（ Landon Hobson ）分享了带薪传教日、读书俱乐部和“制作咖啡”伦理如何帮助普通工人蓬勃发展。
title_zh: 打造让人们茁壮成长的工作场所（与Landon Hobson一起）
content: Landon Hobson is the CEO of Cosmos Corporation, a family business outside St. Louis that makes pet care and household cleaning products sold in 70 countries. With degrees in theology and economics, Landon never expected to run a 250,000-square-foot manufacturing plant—until his father-in-law asked him to take over the company, and he sensed that God had been preparing him for exactly that. Landon describes how his faith shapes Cosmos’s culture: tuition support for any degree an employee wants to pursue, a “Better Book Club” that pays people to read, five paid mission days a year, and a core value of being “willing to make the coffee” for the person behind you. He answers hard questions about whether making dog shampoo really matters to God, and he speaks candidly about the hard years—supply chain disruptions, a drop in sales, and layoffs of people he cared about. He also explains why CEOs need pastors who aren’t passive, and what he has gained from a group of believing business leaders who share the same struggles. Resources Mentioned: To Change the World by James Davison Hunter Every Good Endeavor by Timothy Keller A Public Faith by Miroslav Volf Work in the Spirit by Miroslav Volf
content_zh:
兰登·霍布森(Landon Hobson)是宇宙公司(Cosmos Corporation)的首席执行官,该公司是圣路易斯以外的一家企业,在70个国家销售宠物护理和家庭清洁产品. 凭借神学和经济学的学位,兰登从未预期会经营25万平方英尺的制造厂——直到岳父要求他接管公司,他感到上帝一直在为他做好完全这样的准备.

Landon描述了他的信仰如何塑造宇宙文化:为雇员想要追求的任何学位提供学费支持,一个支付人们阅读费的“更好的书社”,每年有5个付薪的任务日,以及为背后的人“愿意煮咖啡”的核心价值。

他直言不讳地说, 连锁供应中断、销售量下降、以及他所关心的人被解雇。 他也解释了为什么CEO需要不是被动的牧师,

title: Praying for Answers
summary: When Monica’s son Augustine wanted to leave home for a city known for its immorality, she pleaded with God not to let him go. But he went anyway, which greatly grieved his mother, yet it was there that God transformed his life. In his Confessions, Augustine later prayed, “Yet in your deep counsel you heard the central point of her longing . . . [so] that you would make me what she continually prayed for.”
summary_zh: 当莫妮卡的儿子奥古斯丁想离开家到一个以不道德闻名的城市时，她恳求上帝不要让他离开。但无论如何，他还是去了，这让他的母亲非常伤心，但正是在那里，神改变了他的生活。奥古斯丁后来在他的《忏悔录》中祈祷说： “然而，在你深刻的劝告中，你听到了她渴望的中心点……这样你就能使我成为她不断祈祷的东西。”

title_zh: 圣经重生教义（电子书）
content: Edited by John Hendryx in epub , .mobi & .pdf formats Since faith is infinitely beyond all the power of our unregenerated human nature, it is only God who can give the spiritual ears to hear and eyes to see the beauty of Christ in the gospel. God alone disarms the hostility of the sinner turning his heart of stone to a heart of flesh (2 Cor 4:4-6). It is God, the Holy Spirit, alone who gives illumination and understanding of His word that we might believe; It is God who raises us from the death of sin, who circumcises the heart; unplugs our ears; It is God alone who can give us a new sense, a spiritual capacity to behold the beauty and unsurpassed excellency of Jesus Christ. The apostle John recorded Jesus saying to Nicodemus that we naturally love darkness, hate the light and WILL NOT come into the light (John 3:19, 20). And since our hardened resistance to God is thus seated in our affections, only God, by His grace, can lovingly change, overcome and pacify our rebellious disposition. The natural man, apart from the quickening work of the Holy Spirit, will not come to Christ on his own since he is at enmity with God and cannot understand spiritual things (1 Cor 2:14). Shining a light into a blind man's eyes will not enable him to see, because eyesight first requires a set of healthy eyes.
content_zh: 由John Hendryx在Epub编辑, . 惟有上帝解除了罪人将石心变成肉心的敌意(2 Cor 4:4-6). 只有真主,即圣灵,能照亮和理解我们的信仰; 真主使我们脱离罪恶之死,他割取我们的心;他揭开我们的耳朵; 只有上帝才能给我们一种新的感官,一种精神能力,来见证耶稣基督的美丽和无比杰出。 使徒约翰录制了耶稣对尼克德穆斯说,我们自然地热爱黑暗,憎恨光明并不会进入光明(John 3:19,20). 既然我们对上帝的顽强抵抗 被放在我们的慈爱中 只有上帝能以他的恩惠 慈悲地改变 克服并平息我们的叛逆 自然之人,除了"圣灵"的快活活外,不会独自来到基督,因为他对上帝怀有敌意并无法理解精神事物(1 Cor 2:14). 把一盏光照入一个盲人的眼中不会让他看到,因为视力首先需要一组健康的眼睛.

content: by John Flavel Original In ePub , ,mobi & .pdf fomats Modernized In ePub , .mobi and .pdf formats Proverbs 4:23 says to keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life. Our hearts are like fortresses under attack, and we must guard them accordingly. Most people will diligently guard their fortunes and homes, which are of temporal value, but they are very careless about guarding that which is of eternal value their very souls! In this work, originally titled A Saint Indeed, John Flavel (1627 1691) looks at what it means to keep the heart, how to keep the heart, and why keeping the heart is the greatest business of every person. The heart of man is his worst part before it is regenerated—and the best afterward. It is the seat of principles, and the fountain of actions. The eye of God is fixed upon it—and the eye of the Christian ought to be principally fixed upon it.

Professor Berkhof, who was the President of Calvin Seminary and professor of Systematic Theology at the same in the first half of the twentieth century, has given us an excellent compendium of Reformed theological thought in this hefty volume. The subject is treated in the classical style, moving through the Doctrines of God, Man in Relation to God, the Person and Work of Christ, the Application of the Work of Redemption, the Church and the Means of Grace, and the Last Things. For decades, Louis Berkhof’s Systematic Theology has remained one of the most important and widely-used systematic theologies. It provides the clearest and most succinct articulation of Reformed theology. From its first publication in 1932, Berkhof’s work was revised, reprinted, and translated into Chinese, Japanese, Korean, Spanish, and Portuguese, and it had become a standard theological text by 1950. It has gained near-universal use in seminaries and Bible colleges across the world, and is widely cited and used by pastors, theologians, and students of nearly all denominational affiliations.

content: by Thomas Manton in ePub , .mobi & .pdf formats SUCH is the divine matter and admirable order of the Lord’s Prayer, as became the eternal wisdom of God, that composed and dictated it to his disciples. In it are opened the fountains of all our regular petitions, and the arguments contained to encourage our hopes for obtaining them. In our addresses to men, our study is to conciliate their favourable audience; but God is most graciously inclined and ready to grant our requests, therefore we are directed to call upon him by the title of ‘Our Father in heaven,’ to assure us of his love and power, and thereby to excite our reverent attention, to raise our affections, to confirm our confidence in prayer. The supreme end of our desires is the glory of God, in conjunction with our own happiness: this is expressed in the two first petitions, that ‘his name may be hallowed,’ and ‘his kingdom come,’ that we may partake of its felicity. In order to this, our desires are directed for the means that are proper and effectual to accomplish it. And those are of two kinds — the good things that conduct us, and the removal of those evils that obstruct our happiness.

content: by Archibald Alexander In ePub , .mobi and .pdf formats On the basis of fifty years as a pastor, preacher and professor at Princeton Theological Seminary, Archibald Alexander (1772-1851) deals with the subjective work of the Holy Spirit in the heart in all its phases, from the new birth until final preparation for heaven. There are two kinds of religious knowledge which, though intimately connected as cause and effect, may nevertheless be distinguished. These are the knowledge of the truth as it is revealed in the Holy Scriptures; and the impression which that truth makes on the human mind when rightly apprehended. The first may be compared to the inscription or image on a seal, the other to the impression made by the seal on the wax. When that impression is clearly and distinctly made, we can understand, by contemplating it, the true inscription on the seal more satisfactorily, than by a direct view of the seal itself. Thus it is found that nothing tends more to confirm and elucidate the truths contained in the Word, than an inward experience of their efficacy on the heart. It cannot, therefore, be uninteresting to the Christian to have these effects, as they consist in the various views and affections of the mind, traced out and exhibited in their connection with the truth, and in their relation to each other.

content: "Although They Knew God ... They Suppressed the Truth..." The opportunities are wide open for Christians to speak with secular people these days, especially if you live in a metropolitan area. The average hipster you may meet in the medium to big sized city is a secularist who may listen to NPR, has a liberal, ecological, and/or anti-capitalist political ideology ... wears vintage clothing from a thrift store and consumes ethically. He or she often either rides a bike, uses public transportation or even may be driving a hybrid or bio-diesel vehicle. This person is deeply concerned with the ethical treatment of animals, is strongly against slavery, torture, racism and political oppression against women. In other words, he takes morality very seriously. Another characteristic of this individual is that he/she thinks Christianity is irrelevant at best. Since we deeply care about the eternal destinies of such individuals how should we go about reaching such a person with the gospel? Where would you start? Once of the more effective ways, I have found, is to remember that that your secular friend already knows God exists. He/she knows God exists and lives as if He does. In Romans chapter 1 Paul clearly teaches this about all people when he says, "For although they knew God" (verse 21) "...by their unrighteousness suppress the truth" (verse 18). But how can we demonstrate to your friends that they already believe in God, when intellectually they deny His existence? While there are many ways this could be done, I would like to suggest one way that I have found to be quite persuasive: The knowledge of God through their own morality.

title: Don’t Forget the Great Commission When You Counsel
summary: The Great Commission, then, is for fearful, doubting, weak, disbelieving disciples, who need to be reminded of Jesus’s power and authority.   The post  Don’t Forget the Great Commission When You Counsel  appeared first on  9Marks .
summary_zh: 因此，大使命是针对恐惧、怀疑、软弱、不信的门徒，他们需要被提醒耶稣的能力和权柄。当你的律师首次出现在9Marks上时，不要忘记伟大的佣金。

content: Abstract: Nick Gardner reminds pastors of the usefulness of the Great Commission when they counsel church members. Jesus gave the church the task of making disciples, which involves applying his teaching to the sin and suffering of his people. In the midst of trials, disciples of Jesus need to be reminded that their Lord and Savior has all authority in the universe and promises to be with them to the end of the age. John walked into my office again. His head was hanging low. He felt lonely and betrayed by his friends again. Susan was in my office talking about how her boss, a church member, was not easy to work with. David and Joanna were grieving as their wayward child was making poor choices. What do all of these have in common? These are Christians who are suffering and need help. They have been let down, they have been hurt, and they need the Great Commission. The Great Commission? That’s right. Pastor, when you sit across from someone who is suffering from their own sin, from the sin of someone else, or from living in a fallen world, don’t forget the Great Commission. In Matthew 28:18–20, we read, And Jesus came and said to them, “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me. Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you. And behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age.” Remember that the disciples were not exactly brimming with confidence around the time that Jesus spoke these words to them. They had just been: Hiding behind locked doors out of fear of others harming them (John 20:19). Doubting the veracity of the resurrection as told by Mary Magdalene (Luke 24:10). “Startled and frightened and thought they saw a spirit” (Luke 24:37). Doubting the reality of Jesus right in front of them (Matt. 28:17; Luke 24:10–11). The Great Commission, then, is for fearful, doubting, weak, disbelieving disciples, who need to be reminded of Jesus’s power and authority. Here are four reasons to remember these parting words from Jesus as you counsel members of your church through suffering and sin. 1. Jesus Is Sovereign over Everything Echoing Daniel 7:13–14, Jesus makes the startling claim that the entire cosmos belongs to him and is subject to his governing power. This includes the suffering and sin of his people. And this sovereignty comes from his victory over sin and death, for he is the one who healed diseases, hurled out demons, humbled boastful men, and humiliated death. Jesus’s sovereignty is good news because of how he earned it: through his perfect obedience, substitutionary death, and triumphant resurrection. This is the truth you hold out to suffering saints: Christ is ruling and will subdue all their enemies. The authority of Jesus over heaven and earth also includes his authorization of you as a pastor to care for his sheep. As Harold Senkbeil notes, “We have no authorization to do ministry apart from our Lord Jesus. That means we care for the souls entrusted to us according to his express purpose and will.” Harold Senkbeil, The Care of Souls: How to Cultivate a Pastor’s Heart (Lexham Press, 2019), 98. But Jesus isn’t only sovereign over your life; he is sovereign over everything. Suffering has the power to shrink our world from being God’s grand theater of redemption to being more like our walk-in closet of personal suffering. The Great Commission helps us remember that our suffering is not ultimate or all-powerful, as it serves God’s greater purposes in the world. So, pastor, present this bigger picture of God’s supreme authority in your counseling. 2. The Goal of Biblical Counseling Is Making Disciples Biblical counseling is about growth and maturity as a disciple of Christ . content: Abstract : Jonathan Leeman highlights the corporate component of conversion, pointing out that God not only reconciles us to himself through Christ but also to one another. While our (vertical) reconciliation to God is foundational and primary, our (horizontal) reconciliation to others is necessarily bound up with our salvation. Conversion makes us part of God’s people, and this corporate aspect of our salvation should compel us to join a local church. Editor’s Note: This article is taken from Church Matters, the 9Marks journal for pastors, in the issue titled Conversion . If your doctrine of conversion is missing the corporate element, it’s missing something essential. Jesus died for a people (see Mark 10:45). He saves us as individuals, and he saves us into a people. Salvation includes a family. If you’re not convinced, jump straight to these parallel statements from Peter: Once you were not a people, but now you are God’s people; once you had not received mercy, but now you have received mercy. (1 Pet. 2:10) If someone asks you how you became a Christian, you probably emphasize the second line in your testimony. You say something like, “I was living in sin apart from God. A friend shared the gospel with me. I recognized who God is and what Christ did in dying and rising again. Therefore, I repented and believed. Praise God, he forgave me and I received his mercy!” What a wonderful testimony. Don’t stop saying that! Widen Your Perspective But notice that Peter widens the aperture of the camera and tells us a little more about what happened in that same moment. In addition to moving from not mercy to mercy, we simultaneously moved from not a people to a people. That means our testimonies could include a little bit more. Like this: “I was living in sin apart from God, and I wanted nothing to do with God’s family, the church. A friend shared the gospel with me. I recognized who God is and what Christ did in dying and rising again. Therefore, I repented and believed. Praise God, he forgave me and I received his mercy! I also realized that—wow!—I was part of a family now, the church.” Do you see what I mean by the “corporate” component of conversion? We’re saved into the universal church. That’s not to say we should put the corporate element out front. One might think of N. T. Wright’s well-known line about justification being “not so much about soteriology as about ecclesiology; not so much about salvation as about the church . ” N.T. Wright, What Saint Paul Really Said (Eerdmans, 20 1 4), 1 1 9. This is a clear example, in Douglas Moo’s almost-as-well-known line, of backgrounding what the New Testament foregrounds, and foregrounding what the New Testament backgrounds (as cited in D. A. Carson, “Faith and Faithfulness,” Ligonier, February 1 , 20 1 0, https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/faith-and-faithfulness). There can be no true reconciliation between humans until individual sinners are first reconciled to God. The horizontal necessarily follows the vertical. Ecclesiology necessarily follows soteriology. Which is to say, the corporate element must not come first, lest we lose salvation altogether. Vertical and Horizontal But it must come. Indeed, the corporate component must remain within the structure of the doctrine of conversion itself. Our corporate unity in Christ is not just an implication of conversion; it’s part of the very thing. Being reconciled to God’s people is distinct from but inseparable from being reconciled to God. These two elements of conversion are wonderfully put on display in Ephesians 2 with two instances of the word “but.” The first comes as Paul narrates man’s rescue from sin and death (vv. 1–10), which hinges on the words “ But God, being rich in mercy . . . ” (v. 4). Those words introduce God’s saving love and the fact that he has “raised us up with [Christ] and seated us with him in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus” (v. 6).
