title: Help for Beginners and Seasoned Preachers: A Review of David Jackman’s From Text to Teaching
summary: Seeing preaching as a science helps us understand that there are tools we can apply to do the work better. Seeing it as an art reminds us that the work requires us to pay attention to the beauty of Bible proclamation.   The post  Help for Beginners and Seasoned Preachers: A Review of David Jackman’s From Text to Teaching  appeared first on  9Marks .
summary_zh: 将讲道视为一门科学有助于我们理解，我们可以运用一些工具来更好地完成工作。把它看作一门艺术提醒我们，这件作品需要我们关注圣经宣讲的美丽。帮助初学者和经验丰富的传教士：大卫·杰克曼（ David Jackman ）的《从文本到教学》（ From Text to Teaching ）一文首先出现在9Marks上。
title_zh: 初学者和经验丰富的传教士的帮助：大卫·杰克曼从文本到教学的回顾
content: Abstract: Jeremy Meeks reviews David Jackman’s From Text to Teaching: A Guide to Preparing Bible Talks and commends it as a helpful resource for anyone who preaches or teaches the Bible in any context. This brief book offers discussions of the art and science of preaching and the process of preparation, and it provides an inside look at Jackman’s own preparation to preach 1 Corinthians 1–4. The final chapters offer checklists that will be practically useful for preachers, and the appendix contains the author’s own template for preparing a Bible talk. Both beginners and seasoned preachers and teachers will benefit from this book. David Jackman, From Text to Teaching: A Guide to Preparing Bible Talks . Matthias Media, 2021. 92 pp. Even seasoned preacher needs to go back to basics sometimes and be refreshed. Similarly, guys starting out need instruction—someone to teach them how to go about the craft. Often the most helpful teachers are those who have lots of experience. What is even better is if such a preacher has also spent substantial time training others to preach. Ideally, that preacher/trainer has such command of the material that he is able to distill his insights and counsel into a tight, readable book. We have been given such a gift in David Jackman’s little volume From Text to Teaching . In just 92 pages, Jackman provides a lifetime of wisdom for the beginner and the seasoned preacher alike. As he explains in the introduction, he is addressing (as evidenced in the title) the skill of Bible teaching more generally and not solely preaching. This might turn away preachers who don’t consider themselves to be giving “Bible talks,” but that would be the preacher’s loss. The weight of what we get to do every time we open the Bible and teach from it in any context is rightly esteemed by Jackman. The Art and Science of Preaching The book begins by discussing the “Art and Science of Preaching.” Both aspects of preaching—art and science—must be held onto if we are to do it well. Seeing preaching as a science helps us understand that there are tools we can apply to do the work better. Seeing it as an art reminds us that the work requires us to pay attention to the beauty of Bible proclamation. Preaching is more than using the Bible to communicate. Rather, our task is to preach what the text says, that is, giving the meaning of what it says, in context, for the people sitting in front of us. Jackman’s convictions will be new to some, common to others, but beneficial to all. The Process of Preparation A substantial chapter is dedicated to the “Process of Preparation”. Here Jackman helps the Bible preacher/teacher think through how to put a message together. As a preacher who trains other preachers, I’m constantly asked how I do this on a weekly basis, and I enjoy hearing how others do it as well. Jackman has sage advice. He reminds us that we should always be praying (an obvious but seriously neglected aspect of preparation). He is also clear that we should use the time we have strategically. We never have as much time as we would like, and we often think we need more time than we do. The fact is that preachers often waste a lot of time because they are not strategic. Jackman recommends setting aside a few blocks of time in the week (four sessions that are each two to three hours). What is vital is that the preacher figures out what works well for him and plans his schedule accordingly. Jackman then gives helpful advice on how to go about studying and writing out the sermon inside those blocks of time, and this advice is helpful for those at all levels of proficiency. Invited into the Author’s Study The next three chapters (3–5) of the book are pure gold. In essence, Jackman invites us into his study to listen in as he walks through his process of preparing messages on 1 Corinthians 1–4. Here we get insights into how his suggested process works in actual texts. This is something many books on preaching neglect to do, leaving the rea

摘要:杰里米·米克(Jeremy Meeks)评论了大卫·杰克曼的"从文字到教学:准备圣经谈话的指南",并称赞它是任何背景中宣扬或教授圣经的人的有用资源. 这本简短的书提供了对布道的艺术和科学以及准备过程的讨论,它提供了杰克曼自己为布道1科林斯1–4的准备的内观.

最后的章节提供了对传道者实际上有用的核对表,附录中包含了作者自己准备圣经演讲的模板. 初学者和老练的传道人和教师都将受益于这本书。 David Jackman,《从文字到教学:准备圣经会谈指南》,Matthias Media,2021年。

甚至老练的传教士有时也需要回到基础,被刷新. 类似地,开始的人需要教书,有人教他们如何操作这款工艺。 最有帮助的教师往往是经验丰富的教师。 更好的是,如果这种传道者也花大量时间训练其他人传道。

理想的情况是,传教士/教官对材料有如此高的指挥力,他能够将自己的见解和咨询意见提炼成一本紧凑可读的书。 在大卫·杰克曼的"从文字到教学"一书中,我们得到了这样的礼物。 在92页里,杰克曼为初学者和老练的传道者提供了一生的智慧.

正如他在导言中所解释的,他正在讨论(如标题所证明的)《圣经》教学的技巧更普遍,而不仅仅是传道。 这可能会让那些不认为自己在进行“圣经会谈”的传道者退后,

每当我们打开圣经并在任何背景中从中教导时,我们所能做的事情的分量都得到了杰克曼的正确尊重. 该书首先讨论了“影响艺术与科学”。 如果我们要做得好,就必须坚持艺术和科学两个方面的传道。

将传道视为一种科学,有助于我们理解,我们可以应用一些工具来更好地开展工作。 把它看作是一门艺术,提醒我们,这部作品需要我们关注"圣经"宣言的美. 意义不仅仅是用"圣经"来沟通.

相反,我们的任务是宣扬案文所说的话,即在背景上赋予案文所述的含义,供坐在我们前面的人民使用。 杰克曼的信念对一些人来说是新的,对另一些人来说是共同的,但对所有人都有好处。 1. 编写过程

在这里,杰克曼帮助"圣经"的传道人/老师思考如何将一个信息集中起来. 作为一名培养其他传教士的传教士, 我经常问每周我怎么做, 杰克曼有圣人的建议 他提醒我们,我们应当永远祈祷(准备工作中一个明显但被严重忽略的方面)。

他还明确指出,我们应该从战略角度利用我们的时间。 我们从来没有像我们想要的那样多的时间,我们常常认为我们需要比我们多的时间。 事实是道教经常会因为不具有战略意义而浪费大量时间. 杰克曼建议在一周内留出几块时间(每两到三小时四会).

重要的是,传道者要知道什么对他很有效,并据此规划他的时间安排。 杰克曼随后就如何研究并写出这些时间段内的布道给出了有益的建议,而这个建议对于所有水平的熟练程度的人都是有帮助的. 书中接下来的三章(3–5)是纯金.

基本上,杰克曼邀请我们进入他的书房 在他行走的过程中聆听 他准备了科林斯1 -4的信息。 在这里,我们深入了解他建议的进程如何在实际文本中发挥作用。 这是很多书 关于布道 忽略做,留下的灵性

title: Discerning Between Godly and Worldly Grief
summary: Godly grief leads to mourning over sin, not simply its consequences.   The post  Discerning Between Godly and Worldly Grief  appeared first on  9Marks .
summary_zh: 敬虔的悲伤会导致对罪的哀悼，而不仅仅是对罪的后果的哀悼。文章《辨别虔诚与世俗的悲伤》首次出现在九分榜上。
title_zh: 分辨虔诚与世俗的悲伤
content: Abstract: Sam Crites offers three ways to help pastors distinguish between worldly grief and godly grief based on Paul’s words in 2 Corinthians 7:10. Only godly grief produces true repentance, and such grief can be discerned by mourning over sin, not merely its consequences; a genuine desire for reconciliation, no matter the cost; and an earnest desire to please God, not the world. The fruit of godly grief usually becomes evident over time through ongoing repentance and faith in Christ. Editor’s Note: This article is taken from Church Matters, the 9Marks journal for pastors, in the issue titled Conversion . I was discipled by a man named Steve Tucker. He was a simple man full of simple lessons, and one of those simple lessons has stuck with me: a true mark of genuine conversion and its effects is how willing someone is to repent of their sin. However, genuine repentance is a tricky thing. When I catch my children doing something wrong, they are more than willing to “repent,” especially when punishment is imminent. They go from enjoying their wrongdoing to shedding tears. But it’s not always easy to tell if they are grieved over upsetting me or because they know there will be consequences for their actions. Pastors have to make a similar determination when a member is confronted for their sin. Is this person shedding tears only because they were caught in sin, or are they truly repenting? Both kinds of grief can look the same, at least on the surface, but only one leads to life. Those who refuse to repent give evidence that they haven’t been converted. So how can we tell the difference? Three Marks of Godly Grief Since we cannot see the heart of a man, we must look at the fruit of his life—the marks of repentance that accompany genuine conversion. Heart change, not behavior modification, is always the aim. Therefore, we must discern the external evidences of the Spirit’s internal work. This is where Paul’s words to the Corinthians can help us out. He says, “For godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation without regret, whereas worldly grief produces death” (2 Cor. 7:10). Notice that genuine repentance is produced by “godly grief.” Allow me, then, to put forward three marks of repentance from 2 Corinthians 7 that are evidence of godly grief. This list is not meant to be exhaustive but merely a helpful tool for discerning true repentance and, therefore, genuine conversion. 1. Godly Grief Leads to Mourning over Sin, Not Simply Its Consequences In 2 Corinthians 7, Paul describes how restless and anxious he was as he awaited the Corinthians’ response to his previous letter. But when Titus came, Paul was comforted because his report brought news of the grief of the Corinthians—not grief over the harshness of Paul’s letter but grief over their own sin. We’re reminded that godly grief is first and foremost a response to sin and not merely its consequences. David says to God in Psalm 51:4, “Against you, you only, have I sinned and done what is evil in your sight.” How could David be so insensitive? What about Uriah and Bathsheba? Or the child who died? David was aware of how the consequences of his sin affected others, but he felt greater anguish in his heart over how he had offended the Lord. And this should be true for all who repent: they should care most about how their sin has offended their Lord. This is the fruit of understanding the gospel, as the sufferings of Christ on the cross were the payment due for our sin. On the other hand, a preoccupation with the sin of others, a tendency to shift the blame to someone else, or grief that is only short-lived—all these are indications that an individual is not mourning because they have offended the Lord, but instead because of the consequences of their sin. 2. Godly Grief Leads to a Genuine Desire for Reconciliation, No Matter the Cost The Corinthians were grieved that their sin had ruptured their relationship with Paul. title: Why the Doctrine of Conversion Matters for Membership Interviews
summary: It’s difficult to discern whether someone has been converted if you’re hazy on what conversion is.   The post  Why the Doctrine of Conversion Matters for Membership Interviews  appeared first on  9Marks .
summary_zh: 如果你不知道什么是皈依，就很难辨别某人是否已经皈依。帖子Why the Doctrine of Conversion Matters for Membership Interviews首次出现在9Marks上。
title_zh: 为什么转换原则对会员面试很重要
content: Abstract: David Burnette explains why the doctrine of conversion is so crucial for pastors and churches as they carry out their responsibilities in affirming new members as believers. We must not only understand what conversion is but also be able to apply it to the lives of real people. After giving some basic reminders about membership interviews and identifying things that we are not looking for as evidence of conversion, Burnette provides four questions to help us evaluate whether a prospective member has been converted. Editor’s Note: This article is taken from Church Matters, the 9Marks journal for pastors, in the issue titled Conversion . “I wasn’t living right. I was getting drunk, partying, just doing whatever I wanted. And then it was like God just stopped me in my tracks. I knew something had to change. That’s when I started coming to church, and one Sunday, I felt like the preacher was talking directly to me. Right then I knew I needed to become a Christian, and I got baptized a few weeks later. That was about a year ago, and ever since then I’ve pretty much been coming to church and trying to do what’s right.” That’s how Ben responded when you asked him how he became a Christian. Ben recently moved to your city, and he just completed your church’s four-week New Members Class. Now, as the final step in the process—often called a “membership interview”—you as a pastor must decide whether you will recommend Ben for membership at the next members’ meeting. For the purposes of this article, I’m concerned primarily with the question of whether Ben is converted. I’m assuming he meets your church’s other membership requirements. No doubt you’ve heard similar testimonies, even if the details differ. There’s been some kind of change in the person’s life, and they seem sincere, but it’s not yet clear that this change was rooted in the gospel. So you’ll need to do some more probing. Putting Our Doctrine of Conversion to Work Testimonies like Ben’s remind us why having a biblical doctrine of conversion is so crucial when it comes to the church’s responsibility to affirm new members as believers. After all, it’s difficult to discern whether someone has been converted if you’re hazy on what conversion is . For an explanation of the doctrine of conversion, see Michael Lawrence, Conversion (Crossway, 2017); see also the article by Gregg Allison titled “You Can’t Make I t Happen: The Spirit and the Doctrine of Conversion” in this issue of Church Matters . Testimonies like Ben’s also remind us that we must be able to apply our doctrine of conversion to real-life people in real-life situations. Some prospective members will be new Christians, while others will be less mature in their faith; some will have been converted for years but still have significant blind spots; still others will think they’re Christians when they haven’t truly been converted. And those aren’t the only complicating factors. Some will have a hard time articulating the very truths they profess; others will fail to mention basic aspects of the gospel in their interview; more than a few will be unsure as to how and when they recognized their need for a Savior. All these factors (and more) mean that wisdom and discernment are needed when we are interviewing prospective members. Reminders for Our Approach Before thinking through some practical ways to probe further with testimonies like Ben’s, a few basic reminders may be helpful. Your Knowledge Is Limited Unlike Jesus, we can’t look into a person’s heart, which means our decisions about someone’s spiritual state are never infallible. The very fact that Jesus gave instructions about excommunication indicates that he knew the church would sometimes welcome in those who weren’t truly converted (see Matt. 18:15–18). Even the apostle Paul was wrong about his one-time co-worker Demas. Prior to Demas’s departure, Paul mentions him twice when he refers to his fellow workers in the gospel ministry (Col. 4:14; Ph lm. 24). Ou

author: Jeri Choi

title: Unclear Evangelism Leads to Unclear (and False) Conversions
summary: When we appeal to people’s carnal desires, we should not be surprised when our “converts” are more in love with the world than with our Savior.   The post  Unclear Evangelism Leads to Unclear (and False) Conversions  appeared first on  9Marks .
summary_zh: 当我们呼吁人们的肉体渴望时，当我们的「皈依者」更爱世界而不是我们的救主时，我们不应该感到惊讶。“不明确的传福音导致不明确（和虚假）的转换”一文首先出现在9Marks上。
title_zh: 不明确的传福音会导致不明确（和虚假）的皈依
content: Abstract: John Lee explains how bad evangelistic methods and approaches can lead to false conversions. When we are unclear about the urgency of conversion, the cost of conversion, or the accountability that should accompany conversion, we risk leaving people deceived about their eternal state. Ultimately, our job is simply to proclaim the gospel clearly, trust God to open people’s hearts to the truth, and provide ongoing discipleship to those who respond in repentance and faith. Editor’s Note: This article is taken from Church Matters, the 9Marks journal for pastors, in the issue titled Conversion . Maybe you’re like me and you grew up in a church that did altar calls. My church’s zeal for evangelism was real, and I can still tell you the names of individuals who came to know the Lord through those gospel presentations. But like me, you may also have walked down the aisle to accept Jesus as your Lord and Savior at least five times. The thing is, I believe I was sincere every time I walked the aisle. So why do it over and over again? There was clearly a misunderstanding, despite my church’s good intentions—and my own. The methodology of our ministry affects the fruit of our ministry. Or as Mark Dever has put it, “What you win them with is what you win them to .” Unclear invitations often lead to confused converts. Below I want to consider three different ways this lack of clarity in our evangelism manifests itself and how this can lead to conversions that, in time, prove themselves false. Unclear Urgency I was a disobedient kid. When my mother was particularly exasperated, she’d count down from ten. I had a choice: either obey or dig my heels in and rebel. But as I grew older, I became immune to her shot clock and more accustomed to her threats. My mom’s words fell on deaf ears. Bad evangelism capitalizes on this kind of “countdown” strategy. It puts eternity in the balance based on a singular moment and a one-time decision to follow God—or abandon him forever. And while unbelievers may initially respond positively, their “faith” often doesn’t last. As a result, they may become immune to the gospel because they assume they’ve already tried it. “But,” you might say, “isn’t conversion an urgent matter? Do we not care about people’s eternal destiny?” Absolutely! But we want to place appropriate pressure on their conscience, not just on their choice. Unbelievers need to make a thoughtful decision rather than simply meeting our demands in a singular moment in time. Panic urges them to turn off their critical thinking for the sake of survival. The focus is on an immediate decision rather than the weight of God’s eternal judgment. Unclear Cost At the same time, panicked evangelism is sometimes replaced with what we might call chill evangelism. Chill evangelism attempts to downplay urgency in order to make the decision to follow Jesus more palatable. To take one example, some recent invitations have defined following Jesus as “doing as he did.” The call is to adopt his behavior, particularly his compassion toward the brokenhearted. But following Jesus is about more than adopting a certain kind of spirituality and lifestyle; it’s also about salvation from the judgment of a holy God. Nor is it something you can dabble in; it requires real sacrifice. Jesus says in Matthew 10:38, “Whoever doesn’t take up his cross and follow me is not worthy of me.” As Bonhoeffer famously said, “When Christ calls a man, he bids him come and die.” Dietrich Bonhoeffer, The Cost of Discipleship (Simon Schuster, 1959), 89. Conversion costs something. Saying yes to Jesus means saying no to sin, to our own passions, and to our former life. The question is: Does our evangelism draw attention to what people must give up? Conversion doesn’t propel us further toward our goals. Rather, it fundamentally reframes our goals in light of God’s kingdom. When we appeal to people’s carnal desires, we should not be surprised when our “converts” are more in love with the world
content_zh: 摘要:约翰·李(John Lee)解释了糟糕的福音传道方法和方法会导致虚假的转换. 当我们不清楚转换的迫切性,转换的成本,或者在转换时应该承担的责任时,我们冒着让人们对其永恒状态被欺骗的风险. 归根结底,我们的工作只是明确宣示福音,相信上帝为人们打开真理的心扉,并为那些悔改和信仰的人不断提供弟子之道. 编辑说明:这篇文章取自9Marks牧师杂志《教会事务》, 或许你跟我一样, 我的教会对福音的热情是真实的,我仍然可以告诉你通过这些福音演讲来了解主的人的名字。 但和我一样,你也许也走过过道 接受耶稣为主和救世主至少五次 问题是,我相信我每次走过道都是真诚的。 那为什么一遍又一遍? 尽管我的教会有良好意图, 我们部的方法影响了我们部的成果。 或者如马克·迪弗所说的那样,“你以什么赢得他们呢? 不明邀请往往导致混淆的转换. 下面我想考虑一下我们福音派中缺乏明确性的三种不同方式,以及这如何能够导致转变,从而及时证明自己是虚假的。 我是一个不服从命令的孩子 我母亲特别兴奋, 我有一个选择:要么服从,要么挖出我的脚跟来反叛. 但随着我长大了,我变得免疫 她的射钟,更习惯她的威胁。 我妈妈的话听不见。 坏的福音派利用这种“倒计时”战略。 它将永恒置于平衡之中,这种平衡基于一个单一的时刻和一次决定,即顺从真主,或永远抛弃他。 并且虽然不信者一开始会做出正面反应, 因为他们认为自己已经试过了。 " 但是, " 你可能说, " 这不是一个紧迫的问题吗? 难道我们不关心人的永恒命运吗? 当然 但我们要给他们的良心施加适当压力,而不仅仅是给他们的选择。 不信者需要作出深思熟虑的决定,而不是在某一时刻满足我们的要求。 恐慌敦促他们为了生存而停止批判性思维. 重点是立即作出决定,而不是上帝永恒判断的分量。 费用不明 与此同时,惊慌的福音派有时被我们可能称之为寒冷的福音派所取而代之. 冷静的福音派试图贬低紧迫性,以便让决定跟随耶稣更加愉快. 举例来说,最近一些邀请书将跟随耶稣定义为“照他做”。 这个呼吁是采取他的行为,特别是他对心碎者的同情. 但跟随耶稣不仅仅是采取某种精神和生活方式;它也涉及从圣神的判断中取出救赎. 它也不是你能够沉浸在其中的东西;它需要真正的牺牲。 耶稣在Matthew 10:38中说,“谁不拿起十字架跟着我,谁就配不上我。” 正如Bonhoeffer所说:“当基督召唤一个人时,他要他来死。” Dietrich Bonhoeffer,The Cost of Discepleship (Simon Schuster, 1959), 89 (英语). 转换成本很高 对耶稣说"是"意味着对罪恶,对我们自己的激情,以及对我们以前的生活说"不". 问题是:我们的福音派是否引起人们注意人们必须放弃什么? 转换不会推动我们进一步实现目标。 相反,它从根本上根据上帝的王国重新确定了我们的目标。 当我们呼吁人们的性欲时,我们不应该感到惊讶,因为我们的“转变”更加热爱世界。

title: What Conversion Looks Like in Messy People (Like Me)
summary: All sinners, regardless of past trauma, messiness of life, socioeconomic background, or educational attainment must be converted the same way—through repentance and faith in Christ alone.    The post  What Conversion Looks Like in Messy People (Like Me)  appeared first on  9Marks .
summary_zh: 所有罪人，无论过去的创伤、生活的混乱、社会经济背景或教育程度如何，都必须通过悔改和对基督的信心以同样的方式皈依。帖子What Conversion Looks Like in Messy People (Like Me)首次出现在9Marks上。
title_zh: 乱七八糟的人（像我一样）的转化是什么样子
content: Abstract: Mez McConnell points out that the fruit of conversion looks different in everyone’s life, particularly for those who come out of difficult, or “messy,” backgrounds. McConnell illustrates this point by giving two contrasting conversion stories. Then, based on his own background and his ministry among others with difficult backgrounds, he offers five reminders to help pastors minister to such individuals and discern whether they have, in fact, been converted. Editor’s Note: This article is taken from Church Matters, the 9Marks journal for pastors, in the issue titled Conversion . If you’ve been a pastor for a while, it’s likely that you’ve seen some people convert from difficult backgrounds. The Lord saved me from a very difficult past and has given me a ministry to many who come from a similar place. In this piece, I am going to share two conversion stories: one “clean” story and one messy. In God’s kindness to me, I have seen people like John and Jane (who you’re soon to meet) come to saving faith through the witness of my local church. In considering the similarities and differences in John and Jane’s conversions, I pray you grow in boldness, discernment, and patience as you faithfully proclaim the gospel and help people live it out in their own lives. John, a college student who has been attending your Sunday services for some time, asks to speak with you. You meet up and he tells you about his growing conviction over his sin and of his need to repent and place his faith in Christ (those aren’t the terms he uses, but that’s what he means). You feel sure that he is being genuine and so you pray with him and urge him to trust in Christ. Soon after, John tells you that he is now a Christian and so you put him in touch with a mature believer in the church to begin the discipleship process. As the weeks and months progress, you begin to observe a real spiritual hunger in John as he devours the Bible, attends a small group, and comes regularly to a class on Christian doctrine. John begins to pray earnestly in the public meetings, and he volunteers to serve the church body in a number of different ways. So far, so good. John appears to be “soundly converted.” Conversion Doesn’t Always Look the Same Now, let’s change the story to Jane, a single mom of three with an addiction to cannabis and prescription painkillers. What does conversion look like for her? Should we think about “lowering the bar” for people like Jane from so-called “messy” backgrounds? In other words, should we expect less spiritual fruit from Jane than we do from John? And should we expect the spiritual maturation process to be slower, too? Back to Jane and her cannabis and pill addiction. She is in your office talking about feeling convicted of sin and of her desire to put her faith in Jesus for salvation (again, those aren’t the terms she uses, but that’s what she means). As with John, you feel that she is being genuine, and when she tells you a short time later that she’s now trusting in Jesus, you put her in touch with a mature lady in the church to disciple her. However, unlike John, Jane is irregular when it comes to attending Sunday services. Often she turns up late, if she bothers turning up at all. When she does appear, the children are normally loud and fidgety and cause all manner of distractions to those around them. A few members have commented that there is often a strong smell coming off her when she sits near them (later identified as cannabis). When asked about how she is doing spiritually, she becomes very animated about her faith and is proud of the fact that she has drastically cut down her cannabis consumption. The lady who has been discipling Jane reports that she is sporadic in her attendance at Bible study and that she has only been to one small group meeting since professing faith in Christ. You start to have doubts about the genuineness of Jane’s conversion. Things come to a head one evening when a church member calls to inform yo
content_zh: 摘要:Mez McConnell指出,皈依的果实在每个人的生活中都不同,对那些从困难或 " 迷思 " 背景中出来的人来说尤其如此。 McConnell通过给出两个对比的转换故事来说明这一点. 然后,他根据自己的背景以及他的部会和其他有困难背景的人,提出5个提醒,帮助牧师部长向这些人提供帮助,并查明他们是否实际上已经皈依。 编辑说明:这篇文章取自9Marks牧师杂志《教会事务》, 如果你做了一段时间的牧师, 你可能已经看到一些人从困难的背景皈依。 上帝把我从一个非常艰难的过去中拯救出来,并且给了我一个部属给来自类似地方的许多人. 在这部作品中,我将分享两个转换故事:一个是“干净的”故事,一个是混乱的。 我看见约翰和珍(你们很快会见到他们)这样的人, 在考虑约翰和简的皈依过程中的相似之处和差异时,我祈祷你在忠实地宣示福音并帮助人们在自己的生活中生活的同时,以大胆、分辨和耐心地成长。 约翰,一个大学生 他一直在参加你的星期天服务 一段时间,要求与你说话。 他告诉大家,他越来越相信自己的罪过,需要忏悔和信仰基督(这些不是他所用的条件,而是他的意思)。 你确信他是真的 所以你和他一起祈祷 并且敦促他相信基督 不久,约翰告诉你,他现在是基督徒,所以你让他与教会中成熟的信徒联系,开始门徒礼仪过程. 随着数周和数月的进步,你开始在约翰吞噬"圣经"时,观察到一个真正的精神饥饿,参加了一个小团体,并定期来到一个有关基督教教义的班级. 约翰开始在公开会议上真诚祈祷,他自愿以多种不同的方式为教会机构服务. 目前还不错 约翰看来是“貌似被转化了 ” 。 我们改编成Jane的故事, 她的皈依是什么样子? 我们是否应该考虑让Jane这种来自所谓“迷信”背景的人“降低律师资格”? 换句话说,我们是否应该期望简的精神果实比约翰少? 我们是否应期望精神成熟的过程也放慢? 回到简和她大麻和药瘾。 她正在你办公室里谈论被判定有罪的感觉, 以及她希望相信耶稣以救赎的愿望(这又不是她使用的术语, 与约翰一样,你觉得她很真实,当她稍后告诉你她现在信任耶稣时,你让她在教堂里与一位成熟的女士联系,让她成为门徒。 然而,与约翰不同的是,简在参加星期天礼拜时是不规则的. 她经常迟到,如果她烦恼的话。 当她出现时,孩子们通常声音大而虚无,给周围的人带来各种分心。 少数成员评论说,当她坐在他们(后来被确定为大麻)附近时,经常有强烈的气味从她身上冒出. 当被问到她的精神状况时,她变得非常动画化她的信仰,并对她大幅度削减了大麻消费感到骄傲. 这位纪律严明的女士报告说,她偶尔参加《圣经》的学习,自从她表示相信基督以来,她只参加了一次小组会议。 你开始对简的皈依的真实性产生怀疑。 某天晚上,当一个教会成员打电话通知你时,事情就变得头疼了

title: The Reason for Church: A Review
summary: Rescue us from ourselves? No. Jesus died to rescue us from God’s wrath.    The post  The Reason for Church: A Review  appeared first on  9Marks .
summary_zh: 把我们从自己手中解救出来？不，耶稣死是为了把我们从神的愤怒中拯救出来。帖子The Reason for Church: A Review首先出现在9Marks上。
title_zh: 建立教会的原因：回顾
content: Abstract: Paul Alexander reviews Brad Edwards’s book The Reason for Church , highlighting strengths of the book’s cultural diagnosis while also identifying weaknesses in its prescription for how our current problems should be addressed by the church and the gospel. Edwards emphasizes how sin has affected the way we relate to one another, but he does not adequately address the way our sin affects our relationship with God. Readers will benefit from many of Edwards’s insights, but those who believe that the church’s primary mission is to make disciples through the proclamation of the gospel will find substantive areas of disagreement with his view of the church and its mission. Brad Edwards, The Reason for Church: Why the Body of Christ Still Matters in an Age of Anxiety, Division, and Radical Individualism . Zondervan, 2025. 240 pp. When many of us first read David Wells’s No Place for Truth back in the day, we felt like we did when we saw our first Trans Am. You know who you are—don’t deny it. I know, Christian cultural analysis is more than just “cool” or “awesome.” It’s public theology for evangelism. But shouldn’t it be at least a little thrilling to apply Christian logic to public trends? The world never tires of rephrasing the Serpent’s question, “Did God really say . . .?” Our age now rallies around a therapeutic spirituality, justified by victimhood as a new virtue, expressed through social media, aflame with anti-institutionalism. That leaves the local church looking so . . . 1900s, which implies we need not just a reason for God but a reason for church. The title of Brad Edwards’s book, The Reason for Church , tips us off that Edwards hews more to the apologetics of Tim Keller than to the systematics of David Wells. Edwards is an intellectually sophisticated critic of the meta-modern malaise. Thankfully, he loves Christ and the church more than anything in this world. He pastors The Table, a PCA congregation in Colorado that subscribes to the Westminster Confession of Faith. This book earned Christianity Today’s 2025 Book of the Year for its well-informed cultural analysis, penetrating insights, shrewd applications, and flecks of gospel gold. After reading it, I was not surprised to learn The Reason for Church also earned Edwards The Gospel Coalition First-Time Author Award. Edwards turns phrases like pancakes, but he’s not a show-off. He’s heartfelt, and he’s got personal stories from ministry in his own local church that verify and illustrate his analysis and applications. He writes like he’s done this before. Approach Edwards articulates his social critique of late modernity as Burkean conservatism, focused through the political lens of Yuval Levin and Jonah Goldberg, filtered through the sociological insight of Charles Murray, and lit by the psychological findings of Jonathan Haidt. The “little platoons” of local mediating institutions that put us shoulder to shoulder with people across the political aisle are disappearing (79, 93; think Putnam’s Bowling Alone ). We are fracturing the republic into politically homogeneous ghettos by ZIP code. With no buffer between the individual and the political, everything becomes political, impersonal, ultimate . . . and contentious. Diagnosis Today, individualism hijacks individuality such that self becomes sacrosanct. Boomers built churches on Peter Drucker’s pragmatism, which ended up offering Sunday consumers “a Coldplay concert with a TED talk” (14, 16). The church’s customer-is-king technique only manipulates our Main Character Syndrome, making church a provider of goods and services, and excusing us for treating each other as non-player participants in a reality where self is still the star of the show (47–48). Therapy teaches us to prize intuitional over institutional spiritualities (28–35, channeling Philip Rieff and Carl Trueman), so people retreat from churches that call them to repent, choosing instead safe spaces that affirm them in sin. Social media disintegrates
content_zh: 摘要:保罗·亚历山大评论了布拉德·爱德华兹所著"教会的理由"一书,强调了该书文化诊断的优点,同时也指出了该书如何由教会和福音书解决我们当前问题处方的弱点. Edwards强调罪恶如何影响我们彼此的关系,但他没有充分处理我们的罪恶如何影响我们与上帝的关系。 读者将会从爱德华兹的许多见解中获益,但那些认为教会的首要使命是通过宣示福音来培养门徒的人会发现他对于教会及其使命的看法存在实质性的分歧. 布拉德·爱德华兹 《教会的理由:为什么基督的身体在焦虑、分裂和激进个人主义的时代仍然重要》,Zondervan,2025年。 当我们许多人第一次读到大卫·威尔斯的《真理无所归宿》时, 你知道自己是谁, 我知道,基督教文化分析不仅仅是“酷”或“优美”的。 这是福音派的公共神学。 将基督教逻辑运用到公众潮流中, 世界从未厌倦重写蛇人的问题,“上帝真的说过吗?” 我们这个时代现在围绕着一种治疗性精神, 以受害者为理由, 这让当地教会看起来如此 1900年代,这意味着我们不仅需要上帝的理由,还需要教会的理由. Brad Edwards的书标题是《教会的理由》, 爱德华兹是一位在知识上精密的批评者,对"元-现代"的弊病进行了批判. 谢天谢地,他更爱基督和教会,比世界上任何事物都要多. 他在科罗拉多州的一个常设仲裁法院会众中担任牧师,赞同威斯敏斯特信仰忏悔书。 这本书赢得了基督教今日2025年的"年度之书",因为它有丰富的文化分析、深入的见解、精通的应用以及福音黄金的花纹。 在读完之后,我并不惊讶地得知"教会的理由"也获得了爱德华兹福音联盟的"第一次作者奖". Edwards的口味就像煎饼, 他的内心深处, 他写得像以前一样。 接近爱德华兹阐述他对后期现代主义的社会批评为伯克南保守主义,通过尤瓦尔·莱文和约拿·高德伯格的政治透镜来聚焦,通过查尔斯·默里的社会学见解来过滤,并被乔纳森·海德的心理发现所点燃. 当地调解机构的“小排”让我们与政治道上的人并肩并肩(79,93;认为普特南的保龄球是孤独的 ) 。 根据ZIP代码,我们把共和国分裂成政治上单一的犹太区。 在个人和政治之间没有缓冲,一切都变成政治的,非人性的,终极的.和有争议. 今天的诊断,个性主义劫持了个性,以至于自我变得神圣. Boomers根据彼得·德鲁克的实用主义建造了教堂,最终提供星期天的消费者们“与TED谈话的冷戏音乐会”(14,16)。 教会的顾客-王牌技术只操控了我们的主要性格综合症,使教会成为商品和服务的提供者,并责怪我们在现实中将对方视为非玩家参与者,而现实中自我仍然是节目的主角(47–48). 治疗教导我们把直觉的奖赏给制度性精神(28–35,引导菲利普·里夫和卡尔·特鲁曼),因此人们从号召他们悔改的教堂中退缩,选择了安全的地方来证实他们的罪恶。 社交媒体解体
author: Jeri Choi

title: Aiming for Conversion in Our Preaching
summary: Worse than offending unbelievers is treating them like they are believers. Instead, we must aim to help sinners see their sin and confess their need for Christ. This spiritual clarity is not cruel, but kind.   The post  Aiming for Conversion in Our Preaching  appeared first on  9Marks .
summary_zh: 比冒犯非信徒更糟糕的是，像对待信徒一样对待他们。相反，我们必须致力于帮助罪人看到他们的罪，并承认他们需要基督。这种精神上的清晰不是残酷的，而是善良的。在我们的讲道中， “瞄准皈依”一文首次出现在9Marks上。
title_zh: 在我们的讲道中瞄准皈依
content: Abstract: Sam Romine argues that although the preaching that takes place in the weekly gathering should primarily be aimed at believers, pastors should also aim at the conversion of unbelievers in their preaching. He points as evidence to to the prophets of the Old Testament as well as the apostle Paul’s comments about the presence of unbelievers in the gathering in 1 Corinthians 14:23–25. Romine closes with three practical exhortations to help pastors put this into practice. Editor’s Note: This article is taken from Church Matters, the 9Marks journal for pastors, in the issue titled Conversion . Some things are just meant to go together. A warm slice of apple pie with vanilla ice cream. Cozying up with a book on a rainy day. Watching fireworks light up the night sky with a grilled hot dog in hand. Preaching exegetically through a passage and calling for the conversion of sinners—well, that may be taking things a bit too far! As I’ve reflected on preaching with other pastors, it seems there’s a common temptation to underplay preaching for conversion while aiming to preach expositionally as though these two are incompatible or only awkwardly related. Why is this? Some are simply trying to guard against sloppy exposition that ignores the point of the text. Others have been scarred by past experiences of manipulative altar calls and forced invitations, so they seek to distance themselves from these methods. On the other hand, the failure to preach for conversion sometimes arises from biblical convictions. Since the church is for the gathering of believers, why should we take time away from them to tell unbelievers how to have their sins forgiven? Biblical Patterns and Grounds for Preaching for Conversion While I wholeheartedly agree that the Sunday sermon should primarily have God’s people in view, there is biblical precedent to aim for conversion in our preaching. Consider two examples: the Old Testament prophets and the apostle Paul. 1. An Observation from the Old Testament Prophets I love the prophets. They consistently leave me in awe of God’s majesty and glory, as God is shown to be holy and sovereign and, at the same time, kind and gracious. In this they provide a masterful example of how to weave in calls for sinners to repent while still speaking words of correction, comfort, and hope to believers. For instance, nearly all the prophets speak of impending judgment for Israel’s sin and promises of God’s future grace. Hosea pleads with Israel “to return to the LORD your God” (Hos. 14:1). In Joel, God urges the people to “return to Me with all your heart, with fasting, with weeping, and with mourning” (Joel 2:12). Amos calls for the people to “seek the LORD and live,” (Amos 5:4) and Zechariah similarly adds, “Return to me, says the LORD of hosts, and I will return to you” (Zech. 1:3). Of course, Israel is not like the church in that God’s Old Covenant people comprised both believers and unbelievers. Yet we can learn from the way the prophets addressed not only the faithful among God’s people but also those with uncircumcised hearts. God’s concern for the salvation of sinners is demonstrated by repeated calls for repentance. 2. Paul’s Sunday Gathering Observation In 1 Corinthians, Paul addresses several topics pertaining to when believers “come together as a church” (1 Cor. 11:18). Here he makes an important yet often overlooked observation about these gatherings: we are to expect unbelievers to be present. Paul knows the church is made up of those who are “in Christ” (for example, see 1 Cor. 1:2, 4), yet he makes room for the attendance of non-Christians in the weekly gathering. We see this in at least two ways. First, he speaks of “outsiders or unbelievers” entering the gathering when the “whole church comes together” (1 Cor. 14:23). These unbelievers are clearly distinguished from the church. Second, Paul desires the conversion of such people, and he speaks of how powerful it is when unbelievers see God’s people worshipping
content_zh: 摘要:萨姆·罗明(Sam Romine)认为,虽然每周集会中进行的传道活动应主要针对信徒,牧师在传道中也应以皈依不信者为目标. 他向"旧约"的先知以及使徒保罗(Paul)指出,他们认为,在1 Corinthian 14:23–25的集会中,有不信者。 罗明最后提出了三个实际的劝告来帮助牧师将这一点付诸实践. 编辑说明:这篇文章取自9Marks牧师杂志《教会事务》, 有些东西只是要一起走 有香草冰淇淋的苹果派 与一书相会于一雨天. 看着烟花用烤热狗放出夜空中来. 透过一段路, 要求改造罪人, 我考虑过与其他牧师一起传道, 似乎有一种常见的诱惑, 为什么? 有些人只是想防止无视案文要点的草率言论。 另一些人则被过去操纵祭坛和强迫邀请的经历所伤痕累累,因此他们试图与这些方法保持距离. 另一方面,不宣扬皈依有时源于圣经信仰. 既然教堂是供信士们聚会的,我们为什么要花时间告诉不信道的人们,他们的罪过怎么得到宽恕呢? 传承转换的圣经模式和基础 虽然我衷心同意星期天的布道应该让上帝的子民来观望,但我们的布道却有以皈依为目的的圣经先例。 考虑两个例子:旧约先知和使徒保罗. 1. 《旧约》先知的观察,我爱先知。 他们总是让我敬畏上帝的光荣和荣耀,因为上帝被证明是神圣和主权的,同时也是仁慈和仁慈的。 他们以此为表率,说明怎样在劝告罪人悔罪的同时,仍对信士说出改正、安慰和希望的话。 例如,几乎所有的先知都谈到即将对以色列的罪过做出判决,并许诺真主今后给予恩惠。 霍西恳求以色列“回到耶和华你的神身边”(霍斯14:1)。 在乔尔,真主敦促众人“全心全意地归依我,斋戒、哭泣、哀悼”(约尔2:12)。 阿莫斯呼吁人民“向耶和华求生”(Amos 5:4),撒迦利亚同样补充道,“归顺我,万能的耶和华说,我将归顺你”(Zech 1:3)。 当然,以色列与教会不同,因为上帝的旧约中的人既包括信徒也包括不信者。 然而,我们可以从先知们对待上帝人民中的忠实者以及那些有未受洗心的人的方式中吸取教训。 上帝对拯救罪人的关注,表现在一再呼吁忏悔. 2. 保罗的 " 星期日聚会观察 " 在一科林斯,保罗谈到与信徒 " 作为教堂一起来 " (第11:18节)有关的几个专题。 在这里,他对这些聚会作了重要但常常被忽视的观察:我们期望那些不信的人在场。 保罗知道教堂是由那些"在基督中"的人所组成的(例如,见1 Cor. 1:2,4),然而他却为非基督徒出席周会提供了空间. 我们至少从两个方面看到这一点。 首先,他在“整个教堂合在一起”时(第1章第14:23节)谈到“外来者或不信者”进入集会。 这些不信者与教会明显不同. 第二,保罗希望这种人的皈依,他说,当不信道的人们看见真主的百姓崇拜的时候,这种皈依是多么强大。
author: Jeri Choi

title: Eight Enemies of Pastoral Friendship
summary: Biblical friendship is not a luxury for pastors. It is one of God's ordinary means of sustaining us for long-term ministry.   The post  Eight Enemies of Pastoral Friendship  appeared first on  9Marks .
summary_zh: 圣经友谊不是牧师的奢侈品。这是神支持我们长期事奉的常用方法之一。帖子“田园友谊的八个敌人”首先出现在9Marks上。
title_zh: 田园友谊的八个敌人
content: Abstract: Dave Kiehn argues for the importance of friendship for pastors while noting eight different “enemies” that can easily get in the way. These enemies, or obstacles, to pastoral friendships include things like pride, busyness, insecurity, and other issues related to the pastor’s heart and habits. Far from being luxuries, friendships are one of the means God uses to sustain pastors in their work. Pastoral ministry is often described as lonely, but, for most, it doesn’t need to be. From the opening pages of Scripture, God declares that it is not good for man to be alone. Throughout redemptive history, the Lord strengthened his servants through faithful companions. Moses had Joshua. David had Jonathan. Paul had Barnabas, Silas, Timothy, Titus, Luke, and many other fellow laborers. Even our Lord surrounded himself with the Twelve and enjoyed a uniquely close friendship with Peter, James, and John. The church has long recognized the necessity of Christian friendship. Few, though, have captured the beauty of it better than J. C. Ryle: A friend is one of the greatest blessings on earth. Tell me not of money—affection is better than gold; sympathy is better than lands. He is the poor man who has no friends. This world is full of sorrow because it is full of sin. It is a dark place. It is a lonely place. It is a disappointing place. The brightest sunbeam in it is a friend. Friendship halves our troubles and doubles our joys. J. C. Ryle, Practical Religion: Being Plain Papers on the Daily Duties, Experience, Dangers, and Privileges of Professing Christians ( Baker Book House , n.d. ) , 336. Many others have echoed Ryle’s celebration of the blessing of friendship. C. S. Lewis famously observed, “Friendship is born at that moment when one person says to another, ‘What! You too? I thought I was the only one.’” C. S. Lewis, The Four Loves (Geoffrey Bles, 1960), 65. Charles Spurgeon added, “Friendship is one of the sweetest joys of life. Many might have failed beneath the bitterness of their trial had they not found a friend.” Charles H. Spurgeon, “ The Friend of God, ” in The Metropolitan Tabernacle Pulpit , vol. 33 (Passmore & Alabaster, 1887), sermon no. 1938. John Owen reminded us that Christ himself calls us his friends, John Owen, Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost (1657). and Tim Keller observed that the entire history of redemption can be viewed as one great act of divine friendship. Timothy Keller, “Friendship” (sermon, Redeemer Presbyterian Church, May 29, 2005), Gospel in Life, https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/friendship-2/ . Yet if friendship is such a gift, why do so many pastors struggle to cultivate deep, lasting relationships? Sometimes it’s because of a lack of opportunity, though this seems rarer. More often, friendship is lost to enemies in our own hearts and habits. There are definitely more, but here are eight such enemies of friendship to be on the lookout for. 1. Pride: “I Don’t Need Anyone” One of the greatest threats to pastoral friendship, as with any kind of friendship, is pride. Pride whispers to us that mature pastors should be self-sufficient. It convinces us that asking for help is weakness and that admitting struggles will diminish our leadership. Scripture tells a different story. “Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall” (Prov. 16:18). James reminds us that “God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble” (Jas. 4:6). Peter illustrates this danger vividly. Jesus had told him and the other disciples that they would fall away, yet Peter confidently declared, “Even though they all fall away, I will not” (Mark 14:29). Within hours he denied Christ three times. Pride convinces us we are strong enough to stand alone. Humility invites other brothers to speak into our lives before we stumble and fall. The tallest tree is often the first to break when the storm comes. Likewise, pastors who refuse the shelter of faithful friendships often discover their weakness o
content_zh: 摘要:戴夫·基恩认为友情对牧师很重要,同时指出八个不同的“敌人”很容易妨碍他们。 这些对牧人友谊的敌人或障碍包括骄傲、忙碌、不安全以及与牧师的心和习惯有关的其他问题。 友谊远非奢侈,而是上帝用来维持牧师工作的手段之一. 牧师部常被形容为孤独, 真主从天经的开篇中宣布,人独处是不好的。 在整个红色的先发制人的历史中,主通过忠实的同伴来强化他的仆人. 摩西有约书亚。 大卫有乔纳森。 保罗有巴拿巴斯,西拉斯,蒂莫西,提图斯,卢克等许多同事. 甚至我们的主也包围了自己与"十二人",并与彼得,詹姆斯和约翰有着独特的亲密友谊. 教堂早就认识到基督教友谊的必要性. 不过,很少有人比J. C. Ryle更能捕捉到它的美丽:一个朋友是地球上最伟大的祝福之一. 不要告诉我钱——感情比黄金好,同情比土地好。 他是那个没有朋友的可怜人 今出世多为忧恼所生因取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取取. 这是一个黑暗的地方。 这是一个孤独的地方。 这是一个令人失望的地方。 里面最亮的阳光是朋友 友谊将我们的烦恼减半,将我们的喜悦加倍. J. C. Ryle,《实际宗教:成为关于基督教徒日常职责、经验、危险和特权的平凡论文》(Baker Book House, n.d.),336。 许多人响应雷尔对友谊的祝福。 C. S. Lewis著名地观察到,“友谊诞生于一个人对另一个人说:`什么! 你也一样? 我以为我是唯一一个。 ' C. S. Lewis, The Four Loves(Geoffrey Bles,1960),65。 Charles Spurgeon补充说,“友谊是生命中最甜蜜的快乐之一。 许多人如果没有找到朋友,可能在痛苦的审判之下失败了。” Charles H. Spurgeon, “The Friend of God,”载于《大都会Tabernacle Pulpit》, 第33卷(Passmore & Alabaster, 1887年),布道编号:No. 1938 (英语). 约翰 欧文提醒我们,基督自己称我们为他的朋友"约翰·欧文""与上帝同为圣父,圣子和圣灵"(1657年). 蒂姆·凯勒(Tim Keller)指出,救赎的整个历史可以被看作是神圣友谊的伟大行为. Timothy Keller, “友谊” (Sermon, Redeemer Presbyterian Church, 2005年5月29日), 《生命中的福音》, https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/friendship-2. 然而,如果友谊是一种礼物,那么为什么这么多的牧师要努力培养深刻而持久的关系? 有时是因为缺乏机会, 更经常的是,友谊在我们自己的心和习惯中被敌人所失去. 肯定还有更多,但这里有8个这样的友谊敌人需要注意。 1. 骄傲: " 我不需要任何人 " 与任何一种友谊一样,对牧民友谊的最大威胁之一是骄傲. 骄傲地告诉我们,成熟的牧师应该自给自足。 它使我们相信,寻求帮助是软弱的,承认斗争将削弱我们的领导能力。 圣经讲述了不同的故事. “在毁灭前自豪,在倒地前骄傲自大”(第16:18号序言)。 詹姆斯提醒我们,“真主反对骄傲者,但优待谦卑者”(Jas 4.6)。 彼得生动地说明了这种危险. 耶稣告诉过他和其他门徒,他们会掉下去,然而彼得自信地宣称,“即使他们都掉下去,我也不会”(马克14:29)。 几个小时之内 他三次否认基督 骄傲让我们相信,我们有足够的力量独立。 谦卑地邀请了其他兄弟 在我们跌倒前 来谈谈我们的生活 最高的一棵树往往是暴风雨来袭时最先被打破的. 同样,拒绝为忠诚的友情提供庇护的牧师也常常发现他们的弱点。

title_zh: 非洲花园中的新蛇
content: ABSTRACT: Just as the serpent led Adam and Eve into idolatry by reinterpreting God’s good word, so prosperity and word-of-faith preachers are today proclaiming a false and idolatrous gospel. But unlike Adam, African preachers are refusing to stay mute. Recognizing the need for faithful interpretation of Scripture, they have drawn up a statement to help pastors stand against the idolatrous assumptions and teachings of the prosperity gospel and word-of-faith theology. For our ongoing series of feature articles for pastors and Christian leaders, we asked Dieudonné Tamfu (PhD, Southern Baptist Theological Seminary), pastor of Église Baptiste Bethléem and Assistant Professor of Bible and Theology and Director of the Cameroon Extension Site of Bethlehem College and Seminary, to introduce readers to the recently published Africa Statement on the Prosperity Gospel and Word of Faith Theology . Christian leadership is war. When God calls a man to shepherd his flock, he calls him to war against wolves. Satan, the father of lies, and his minions hate the spiritual health of God’s people, wanting nothing more than to lead the people of God from truth to idolatry. The spiritual leaders of God’s flock are called to fight against Satan’s counterfeit gospels by proclaiming the word of God (Ephesians 6:17). When those leaders fall silent, when they fail to preach the sufficiency of Christ alone, they make space for Satan to lead the people of God into idolatry. As John Calvin rightly said, “Those in authority in the church turned over to idols the office of teaching for no other reason than that they themselves were mute.” 1 The muteness of faithful leaders gives voices to idols. Since Genesis 3, the devil has been in the business of poisoning the minds of God’s people with lies. In God’s good garden, the enemy came preaching lies: If God truly loves you, he will give you the fruit from the tree in the middle of the garden. Eve paid close attention while Adam idly stood by, mute. Thus he, his wife, and all his descendants died of the poison of Satan. The world is under the curse of sin because of a failure of leadership. 2 One of Satan’s most deceptive counterfeits plaguing both American and African churches is the prosperity gospel, a false teaching that elevates the idols of health, wealth, and power. David Oyedepo, a strong proponent of the prosperity gospel and word-of-faith theology, says, “Healing is the covenant right of every child of God . . . sickness has no right to feast on your life.” He goes on to proclaim healing over his congregation: “In the name of Jesus, I decree an end to every toil with sickness and disease.” He assures them that faith in Jesus means the end of sickness. 3 As I’ve written elsewhere, this “idolatrous perversion of the gospel” turns Jesus into “a means to God’s full blessings, primarily of health, wealth, and might” in the present life. 4 Its widespread success indicates a failure on the part of so-called shepherds to engage in spiritual warfare by speaking the whole testimony of God’s word. Today, many church leaders in Africa are boldly refusing to remain mute while the “new serpent,” the prosperity gospel and word-of-faith theology, reinterpret God’s goodness as mere material blessings. These bold leaders are now advancing the centrality of the true gospel by the recent publication of the Africa Statement on the Prosperity Gospel and Word of Faith Theology . The present essay introduces the statement, first explaining why it is necessary, then summarizing its main points, and concluding with a warning against the syncretism of prosperity teaching. Hermeneutical Battlefield Our hermeneutics determine whom we hallow, and whom we hallow reinforces our hermeneutics. As it was in the garden, the fight for the people of God is the battle for faithful interpretation of God’s word. content: Audio Transcript We like to think in simple categories. It’s easier that way, and easier to be clear in explaining things. So, if I ask, “How are you doing?” you will probably respond in terms of “good” or “bad,” and then explain why you are feeling good or bad. By default, we are doing fine until we are doing bad, but it’s normally one or the other, up or down like a light switch: We’re good. We’re bad. Then along comes the apostle Paul and pulls this on-off switch off the wall and breaks it into pieces to teach us that the very good and the very bad coexist in this life. Today on Ask Pastor John: the many flavors of holy joy. It’s a question from an anonymous listener to the podcast. “Pastor John, you have been writing and speaking for decades about the importance of joy in the life of God and the life of a Christian. You have made the case that joy in God — not only in his gifts but in his person — is essential to glorifying God. You have argued that the reason that God’s God-centeredness, his pursuit of his own glorification in all he does, is not megalomania is precisely because he magnifies his glory through our enjoyment of him. You have pointed out that the apostle Paul not only spoke of being ‘sorrowful, yet always rejoicing,’ but that he also said, ‘In all our affliction, I am overflowing with joy’ (2 Corinthians 6:10; 7:4). That last statement seems staggering. If it can be present in such different circumstances, can you help me even begin to imagine what true joy is?” Joy in All Circumstances That very statement from 2 Corinthians 7:4 has arrested my attention for a little over a year (since I taught 2 Corinthians last year) and just wouldn’t let me go, because it seems to demand that we dig into the nature of joy to figure out what he could possibly mean by calling his experience joyful in the light of so many different sufferings. He mentions 26 sufferings, different kinds of affliction in 2 Corinthians 11:23–28. It’s not just Paul’s experience of joy in all those afflictions that drives me, but many, many different circumstances in the Bible are the circumstances in which we are told to rejoice. It’s just incredible how many there are. Here are a few. - Rejoice in your future inheritance (1 Peter 1:3–6). - Rejoice that your names are written in heaven (Luke 10:20). - Rejoice in the plundering of your property for love’s sake (Hebrews 10:34). - Rejoice in being poured out for others (Philippians 2:17–18). - Rejoice in spending and being spent for souls (2 Corinthians 12:15). - Rejoice in your weakness for Christ’s sake (2 Corinthians 12:9–10). - Rejoice in being slandered and persecuted and rejected (Matthew 5:11–12; Luke 6:22–23). - Rejoice in being shamed for Christ’s name (Acts 5:41). - Rejoice in contributing to others’ needs (2 Corinthians 9:7). - Rejoice in the partnership of other believers (Philippians 1:4–5). - Rejoice in people being converted (1 Thessalonians 2:19–20). - Rejoice in the unity of believers (Philippians 2:2). - Rejoice in truth (1 Corinthians 13:6). - Rejoice in the law of God (Psalm 119:14, 111, 162). - Rejoice in the Lord (Philippians 4:4). - Rejoice in the hope of the glory of God (Romans 5:2). - Rejoice in God (Romans 5:11). That’s for starters. The variety of circumstances in which we are told to rejoice demands this: Joy is not a static emotion but one that changes in intensity. That’s pretty obvious for everybody, but also — this is what I’m drawing out now that feels fresh to me — it varies in quality. So, what do I mean by quality? I mean the nature or the kind of experience joy is — not just how intense it is but how different it is, or how it can feel so different from one kind of experience to the next. And yet, all of them could be called joy, which I think means a positive emotion that we really want to have. That would be my kind of bottom-line definition of joy. title_zh: 你就不能让我去参加吗？
content: We live in a chronically noncommittal society. No wonder, then, that this has been dubbed the age of anxiety. Surely, covenant relationships aren’t the only cure, but it might surprise us how much stability of soul comes from deep, reliable, unflighty fellowship. Today, most of the mainstream societal influences in your life implicitly or explicitly cater to your personal sense of freedom. Change your mind, opt out, you do you. No need to cut ties if you don’t have them. Many of the freedoms we enjoy in late modern life are truly precious gifts — some even generally conducive to true Christianity. But others subtly promote a false vision of self and all reality; they pretend (and we’re often happy to pretend along with them) that our autonomous selves are the end-all-be-all. I am the given; others should cater to me. My immediate desires are fixed; the world around me should adjust accordingly. Covenant-Making God Into this pit of quicksand enters the covenant-making God. That you are a creature, who did not make yourself, but was made (and is upheld) by the Creator, is bracing enough. Add to that, he’s not just God but a God who makes covenants. God made a covenant with the first man in the garden before sin entered the world and dwelled in the human soul. God made a covenant with a moon-worshiper named Abraham and promised to make a nation out of him. God made a covenant with that nation of chosen people once he had delivered them safely from slavery. And this covenant was not simply with him vertically but included thick horizontal commitments to fellow humans for life together under God. Today, we orient in and under Christ through the new covenant . From it follow horizontal commitments to each other, promises worked out, inevitably, among real people in our own locale, that is, in local churches. The wisdom and power of local church “membership” (or whatever you call it) rests not on a single proof text or two. Rather, the nature of human relationships in the world God made, the arc of redemptive history toward a new-covenant people not of ethnic birth but delivered from sin and death by new birth, the good limits of creaturely finitude particularized in various places around the world — all these lead inexorably to “membership,” specific people committed to one another in a specific place. No matter what you call it, what’s vital is the concept of real belonging and mutual allegiance. My Sheep? In a recent essay , Massachusetts pastor Stephen Witmer defines “church membership” as a clear and continuing mutual commitment between an individual Christian and a local church, in which the church endorses the member’s profession and shepherds the member’s soul, and the member submits to the church’s authority and shares in the church’s life. The implicit commitment between churches and their duly appointed leaders in the New Testament provides a compelling line of evidence for “membership.” Hebrews refers to Christians having their own local leaders, who keep watch over their souls (Hebrews 13:17). The benefits here are mutual and manifold. Humble Christians want leaders who know them in their local setting and watch over their souls. And good leaders, to do their work, need to know whom they will give account for — who’s in and who’s out. The apostle Paul addresses the local leaders in Ephesus, saying, “Pay careful attention to yourselves and to all the flock, in which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers” (Acts 20:28). To give the flock their careful attention and watch out for their souls, shepherds need to know who’s in the flock and who’s not. In the same way, the apostle Peter tells leaders in Rome to “shepherd the flock of God that is among you, exercising oversight . . . not domineering over those in your charge, but being examples to the flock” (1 Peter 5:2–3). content: I’m excited to tell you the story of how God used a simple verse, from a complicated passage, to change the life of a man named Charles Spurgeon. His story is for everyone, but it may have a special word to speak to a few groups in the room. One is laymen — that is, people who work for a living in normal jobs, outside of Christian ministry. People without a seminary education, people who aren’t pastors or have ministry jobs. We recognize that this series has profiled four men who were preachers. Now, there is an interesting flow to our series: - first, Saint Augustine, - then, Luther, who was an Augustinian monk, - then, John Bunyan, whose favorite book outside the Bible was Luther’s commentary on Galatians, - now, Charles Spurgeon, whose favorite book outside the Bible was Bunyan’s Pilgrim’s Progress. We’ve moved from one convert to another, each building in some way on the previous one, but a weakness of our series (in some sense) is that they all became preachers. And we don’t expect you all to become preachers; we’d like a few, but most will be laymen, and that’s good. Now, Spurgeon is known as “the Prince of Preachers.” But the hero, under God, in Spurgeon’s story is not Spurgeon, and not a trained, paid preacher, but a layman. So, Spurgeon’s story has a special word for laymen who are willing to open their mouths and say what they know about Jesus. Spurgeon’s story also has a special word for teens and young adults. Spurgeon came to faith at age fifteen, which in his day was far more like young adulthood. Still, his story offers a challenge to those who are no longer children and not yet established adults: teens, college students, grad students, even young professionals. Don’t let the world (or the church) lower your standards of what’s possible in being deeply converted and dedicated to Jesus — and how God can make his Son thrilling to a young soul. My prayer is that God might be pleased to give some their own engine. So often, parents, college workers, and pastors help young adults along and give them pushes. And then sometimes, God is pleased in the life of teenagers to give them their own engine, and they don’t need any more pushing. They say, “Get out of my way! I am going to follow Jesus. You can’t keep me from him and worship, my Bible, and prayer!” That’s what God did for Spurgeon at age fifteen — he gave him his own engine. And I pray he might be pleased to do that even here this morning. Spurgeon’s story speaks to one more group: those in the room who are willing to admit, “I’m here but I’m not saved.” For two thousand years, unsaved people have shown up at churches for all sorts of reasons. That’s Spurgeon’s story. He was searching. He was unsaved and in a church on a Sunday morning when God broke through. So, if you’d say this morning, “I haven’t settled the issue of my sin and rebellion against God,” or “I haven’t ‘been saved,’” or “if I died on the drive home today, I wouldn’t be at peace with my Maker,” this story has a special word for you. So, let me tell you about Charlie Spurgeon. His Early and Whole Life He was born in 1834, about 40 miles northeast of London, into a Christian family. In fact, both his father and grandfather were pastors. But his father met financial troubles and sent the young Charles to live with his grandparents from ages one to six. I don’t think this is an insignificant part of the story; don’t underestimate the effects of a good grandma and grandpa in the lives of our children. From their influence he emerged as “precocious,” learned to read, and first found Bunyan’s Pilgrim’s Progress (which he would read more than a hundred times). From his earliest days, he was unusually sharp, ahead of his age level, “always reading books” (Spurgeon: A Biography, 8). He returned home at age six and excelled at school in both math and reading. He was noticed for “his unusual mental ability and his rare clarity of speech” (10), including “his native audacity” (11), that is, his courage to say

没有神学院教育的人, 我们承认,这一系列的描述 4人谁是传道者。

现在,我们的系列有一个有趣的流传:首先,圣奥古斯丁, 然后,路德,他是一个奥古斯丁的修道士, 然后,约翰·邦扬,他最喜欢的书是路德对加拉提安的评论, 现在,查尔斯·斯普吉翁,他最喜欢的书是"邦扬朝圣者的进步"。

斯普吉安在15岁时开始信仰,在他这一天,这更像是年轻的成年. 然而,他的故事给那些已经不是孩子和还没有成年的人带来了挑战:青少年,大学生,研究生,甚至年轻专业人员.

content: As we were finishing a counseling session, Jill looked at me with concern, her eyebrows furrowed. “You got distracted,” she bluntly stated. Unfortunately, Jill was right. Just outside my workspace, several pastors gathered in the church office lobby, talking and laughing. I’d gotten sidetracked by the commotion. About 70 percent of me was attending to Jill, but 30 percent of my headspace had shifted to the lobby: What are they doing? What’s so funny? We live in a distractible culture. Between YouTube shorts and checking our email inboxes every hour, our minds wander quickly. Staying focused is a skill few truly master. But it’s essential if we’re going to care well for God’s people. Whether formally or informally, counseling another soul is a distinct privilege. Yet, too often, mistakes plague our conversations. Fortunately, getting distracted is one of several common mistakes that are correctable. After Jill’s jarring comment, I closed the window blinds (simple fix), talked to the staff about keeping the commotion down (another simple fix), recommitted to staying focused (possible, though it would be work), and prayed the Lord would renew my love for his sheep. What counseling mistakes are you prone to make? Take a quick check. Mistake 1: Fear of Man Charlotte shares about her struggles with her job. She dislikes her boss, and she’s weary of her work. Unfortunately, she often responds to her difficulties with sinful choices. This time, she lied to her boss to get out of an assignment. You sympathize with her frustrations but feel convinced you’ve got to speak up about her lying. Charlotte’s a Christian, and Scripture makes clear that because God never lies, Christ’s followers shouldn’t either (Colossians 3:9–10; Titus 1:2). Yet you hesitate. You know Charlotte will get angry, and your fears kick in. Why bother bringing it up? Lying is between her and God. Right now, she needs a friend. But you know if you don’t say something, Charlotte will eventually lie to her boss again. What should you do? Repent of your fear that causes you to avoid a difficult word. Confess your worry about speaking up to the Lord (Psalm 34:4). If you struggle with people-pleasing, then saying a difficult word will feel painful. Reframe your situation by putting the fear of God at the center of your thinking (Proverbs 29:25; Luke 12:4–5). If we fear God more than Charlotte, we won’t let Charlotte’s potential anger get in the way. My friend Jonathan Leeman calls the helper in this situation a “sin-absorber.” A true friend willingly absorbs the cost of another person’s sin for the sake of honoring Christ. Would you be willing to absorb Charlotte’s anger if it helps her address her lie? Mistake 2: Assumed Insight Angela and John have been married for 31 years. Sometimes John gets frustrated with Angela because she assumes what he’s thinking. “I know I’m not supposed to assume,” Angela would think, “but we’ve been together for a long time.” The more familiar you are with someone, the more you’re likely to get in trouble. Familiarity breeds assumptions . Think about your last conflict. How many assumptions did you make? Probably a few. Assumptions can create problems. Sometimes our assumptions are true, but often they’re not. If you’re prone to making assumptions, here’s how to stay away from trouble: Don’t overestimate your ability to size up a situation. Pride makes you think, “I know what’s going on.” Humility tells you, “Ask God for wisdom.” The humble recognize they’re not as smart as they think and must depend on the Lord for insight (James 1:5). After you’ve asked the Lord for help, test your assumptions. Don’t tolerate any of them. Check the validity of your assumptions by asking thoughtful, careful, and loving questions. Genuine curiosity will lead you to ask rather than assume. At the encouragement of a friend, Angela asked more questions during marital conflict, and that built more understanding between her and John. The apostle Paul tells us that

content: What marks Christians attuned to cross-cultural missions? They may not serve as full-time missionaries, but they embrace Great Commission responsibilities. The history of missions reveals little-known senders who used their vocations for strategic gospel advance around the world. Captain Benjamin Wickes (1746–1830) was one such man. ‘Old Captain Wickes’ We meet this early American captain of a merchant vessel unexpectedly at a prayer meeting in 1806. The missionaries in Serampore, India, had gathered to send Henry Martyn to a station on the Ganges River where he would begin his work of translation and evangelism. Martyn recorded that they “met at my pagoda this evening for the purpose of commending me to the grace of God before my departure. My soul never before had such divine enjoyment” ( The Letters of Henry Martyn , 194). I would love to have been there. The meeting included both Baptist missionaries — William Carey, Joshua Marshman, and William Ward — as well as evangelical Anglicans David Brown, Daniel Corrie, and Henry Martyn. It represented a substantial collaboration between these earliest English missionaries for the advance of the gospel in India. Since much of India was controlled by the British East India Company, only Anglican missionaries received official recognition and freedom to travel. Even they, however, could pursue missionary work only when not employed in chaplaincy duties to English people residing in India. Amid such challenges, this prayer meeting of gathered co-laborers was a high point for Martyn and a moment he remembered fondly. To the list of those present, Martyn added “old Captain Wickes.” He mentioned him again in another letter as “the good old Captain Wickes, who has brought out so many missionaries to India” ( Letters , 178). But who was this old American captain so well loved by the English missionaries in India? Missionaries as Risky Passengers Captain Wickes was born to a seafaring family in Maryland in 1746. His older brother, Captain Lambert Wickes, fought and died at sea during the American War for Independence. Benjamin first entered the missionary record in 1799, when the Baptist missionaries Joshua Marshman and William Ward sought passage to India from London. The situation was sensitive. The East India Company had forbidden full-time missionaries from entering, so no English ship would give Marshman and Ward passage. Carey had established his home in the Danish port of Serampore, not far from Calcutta, but no Danish ships were available. Wickes’s American ship, however, could take the risk of transporting missionaries. When he heard about the situation, Wickes wrote to Baptist leader Andrew Fuller, saying that “he had long cherished the hope of being privileged to convey the messengers of the Gospel to the heathen, and that his fondest wish was about to be gratified” ( The Life and Times of Carey, Marshman, and Ward , 110). The privilege came with difficulties. Although American ships were regularly received in East India Company ports, the presence of missionaries complicated their arrival. When Wickes arrived in Calcutta with Marshman and Ward, East India Company officials refused him permission to sail home unless he took the missionaries with him. By God’s grace, Wickes convinced the authorities of the missionaries’ good intentions. When similar circumstances occurred in 1806, he persuaded officials that detaining his American ship might cause an international incident. Each voyage involved protracted negotiations that certainly distracted from his primary trading business. Yet Wickes’s service proved invaluable. Every time the missionaries mentioned him, they affirmed their unbridled thanks for his efforts. William Carey wrote about him in 1805, “I, in common with my dear brethren and sisters here, feel much pleasure in hearing of the safe return to you of our much beloved brother in Christ, Capt. Wickes” ( Evangelical Intelligencer , 1:201). Marshman and Ward called him “th

威克船长 在1806年的一次祈祷会中,我们意外地遇到了这位早期的美国商船船长. 印度塞兰波尔的传教士们聚集一堂,将亨利·马蒂恩送往恒河上的一个站,在那里他将开始翻译和福音派的工作.

Martyn记录说,他们“今晚在我的佛塔相会,目的是在我离开之前赞扬我受到上帝的恩惠。 我的灵魂从未有过如此神圣的享受”(The Letters of Henry Martyn, 194). 我很想去过那里。

与会的有浸信会传教士威廉·凯里(William Carey),约书亚·马什曼(Joshua Marshman)和威廉·沃德(William Ward)等,还有福音派圣公会教徒大卫·布朗(David Brown),丹尼尔·科里(Daniel Corrie)和亨利·马蒂恩. 它代表了这些最早的英国传教士为在印度推进福音而进行的实质性合作。

由于印度大部分地区被英国东印度公司所控制,只有英国圣公会传教士才得到官方的承认并享有出行的自由. 然而,即使他们也只能在不受雇于居住在印度的英国人担任牧师职务时才能从事传教工作。

在这样的挑战中,这次聚集的同实验室的祈祷会是马蒂恩的高潮,也是他亲切回忆的一瞬. 在出席者名单中,马蒂恩加上了“威克船长”。 他在另一封信中再次提到他,称他为“威克船长,他把这么多传教士带到了印度”(信件,178)。

但这位老美国队长 在印度的英国传教士这么爱谁? 传教士作为"冒险乘客""威克船长"于1746年生于马里兰的一个航海家庭. 他的哥哥,船长兰伯特·威克斯(Lambert Wickes)在美国独立战争中出战并死于海上.

本杰明于1799年首次入传教记录,当时浸信会传教士约书亚·马什曼和威廉·沃德从伦敦寻求通向印度. 情况很敏感。 东印度公司曾禁止全职传教士入道,因此英国船只不会给马什曼和沃德通过.

凯里在离加尔各答不远的丹麦塞兰波尔港建立了他的家,但是没有丹麦船只可供使用. 但威克斯的美国船可能承担运送传教士的风险。

当Wickes听说情况时,他写信给浸信会领袖Andrew Fuller,称“他长期以来一直珍视着有幸将福音信使传达给异教徒的希望,而且他最亲切的愿望即将得到满足”(The Life and Times of Carey, Marshman, and Ward, 110.). 特权带来了困难。

虽然美国船只经常被接收到东印度公司港口,但传教士的到来使其更加复杂. 当威克斯与马什曼和沃德一起到达加尔各答后,东印度公司官员拒绝他出航回家,除非他带着传教士一起. 在上帝的恩典下,威克说服了传教士的善意权威.

当1806年发生类似情况时,他劝说官员们,扣留他的美国船只可能造成国际事件. 每次航行都涉及旷日持久的谈判,当然分散了他的初级贸易业务。 但威克斯的服务证明是宝贵的。 每逢传教士提到他,他们都申明他们无所顾忌地感谢他的努力.

title: How Did the Gospel Get to Pakistan?
summary: Selah Lipsey traces the history of Christianity in Pakistan and explores how the church continues to grow despite persecution.
summary_zh: Selah Lipsey追溯了巴基斯坦的基督教历史，并探讨了尽管遭受迫害，教会如何继续发展。
title_zh: 福音是如何传到巴基斯坦的？
content: Out of a population of 219.9 million , an estimated 3.3 million people in Pakistan claim to be Christians. As we consider the Church today, we can gain insight by looking back in history to see how and when the gospel was first brought to Pakistanis. So, how did Pakistan get to this point? HOW WAS THE GOSPEL BROUGHT TO PAKISTAN? The gospel may have first reached what is now Pakistan as early as the first century AD. Traditions holds that the Apostle Thomas traveled east to share the gospel, possibly reaching Taxila, an ancient city in modern-day Pakistan. But historians disagree about whether Thomas visited this region, and there is no conclusive evidence of a Christian community in the area dating back to that time. By the late 1500s, there was a more clearly documented presence of Christianity when Jesuit missionaries traveled to the Mughal Empire . Emperor Akbar invited Christian missionaries to his court for religious discussions. By the 1590s, Jesuits had established a presence in Lahore—the capital of the Mughal Empire and part of modern-day Parkistan—and built a church there. However, these early Catholic missions had limited long-term impact. In the 19th century, the most influential growth of Christianity occurred when Protestant missionaries began establishing churches, schools, and other ministries in the country, particularly in Punjab. These efforts helped lay the foundations for many of Pakistan’s Christian communities today. WHAT DOES THE CHURCH LOOK LIKE TODAY? Today, less than 2% of Pakistan’s population identifies as Christian within the predominantly Muslim country. Pakistan’s identity as an Islamic state is central to understanding the situation of Christians today. In 1947, Pakistan was created through the partition of British India. Pakistan became a homeland for Muslims of the subcontinent, amid deep religious and political tensions. In 1956, Pakistan formally became the Islamic Republic of Pakistan. The country’s 1973 constitution established Islam as the state religion and required laws to conform to Islamic principles. Although the constitution guarantees citizens the right to practice and profess their religion, Islam holds a privileged position in the country’s legal and political system. Being a Christian in Pakistan can come with significant social and personal risks. Christians can face discrimination, economic marginalization, and pressure because of their faith. Pakistan’s blasphemy laws also create serious risks, including imprisonment, threats, or violence. Christians who convert from Islam may face hostility and disownment from family and their community. Because of this pressure, many believe that the number of Pakistani Christians may be higher than 2%. Many believers choose to live in secret due to persecution. But despite these challenges, Christians continue to share their faith and gather as the Church. HOW CAN YOU PRAY FOR THE CHURCH IN PAKISTAN? With 96% of Pakistan’s population identifying as Muslim, pray for the gospel to be heard and for salvation through Christ alone to be known and believed. Pakistani Christians often face violence, and they live under laws that make it difficult to share the gospel. Pray for their safety and for them to be bold in sharing their faith. Pray for believers from an Islamic background to be strengthened in their faith and encouraged by their brothers and sisters in Christ, as many will lose their family and friends. Pray for Radical’s partnership to train young believers and church leaders from rural areas in Pakistan. The goal is to encourage them, train them in biblical understanding, and to equip them for evangelism among Muslims. These believers are trained and strengthened through Bible studies, teachings, and one-on-one counseling. As we pray to see the church grow in Pakistan, we also pray for the next generation of church leaders and believers to be equipped with a firm foundation and with evangelism skills.
content_zh:
在2.199亿人口中,巴基斯坦估计有330万人自称基督徒。 在我们今天考虑教会时,我们可以回顾历史,看看福音是如何和何时首次传到巴基斯坦人的。 那么,巴基斯坦是如何达到这一步的? 如何是政府带巴基斯坦?

福音可能早在公元一世纪就已经到达现在的巴基斯坦。 传统认为使徒托马斯向东行走分享福音,可能到达了巴基斯坦近代古城塔克西拉. 但历史学家对托马斯是否访问这一地区有不同意见,没有确凿证据表明该地区有一个基督教社区可以追溯到那个时代.

到1500年代后期,耶稣会传教士出行到莫卧儿帝国时,基督教的存在有了更明确的记载. 阿克巴尔皇帝邀请了基督教传教士到他的宫廷进行宗教讨论. 到1590年代,耶稣会已经在拉合尔(即莫卧儿帝国的首都和近代帕克斯坦的一部分)建立了存在,并在那里建造了一座教堂.

然而,这些早期的天主教传教活动产生的长期影响有限. 19世纪,基督教最有影响力的成长发生在新教传教士开始在国内,特别是在旁遮普建立教堂,学校等部会. 这些努力有助于为当今巴基斯坦的许多基督教社区打下基础。

查克今天长什么样? 今天,不到2%的巴基斯坦人口在以穆斯林为主的国家内认定为基督教徒。 巴基斯坦作为一个伊斯兰国家的身份对于理解当今基督徒的处境至关重要。 1947年由英属印度分治而来巴基斯坦.

巴基斯坦成为次大陆穆斯林的家园,处于严重的宗教和政治紧张局势中. 1956年,巴基斯坦正式成为巴基斯坦伊斯兰共和国. 1973年的宪法将伊斯兰教确立为国教,并要求法律符合伊斯兰原则.

虽然《宪法》保障公民信奉和信奉宗教的权利,但伊斯兰教在该国的法律和政治制度中占有特权地位。 身为巴基斯坦的基督徒, 基督徒可能因其信仰而面临歧视、经济边缘化和压力。

巴基斯坦的亵渎法也造成了严重的风险,包括监禁、威胁或暴力。 皈依伊斯兰教的基督教徒可能面临敌意并脱离家庭和社区。 由于这种压力,许多人认为巴基斯坦基督徒人数可能高于2%. 许多信徒由于被迫害而选择秘密地生活.

但尽管面临这些挑战,基督徒仍继续分享信仰并聚集为教会. 你怎么能为巴基斯坦 Church祈祷? 巴基斯坦96%的人口都认同为穆斯林,他们祈祷能够听到福音,祈祷仅仅通过基督就能得到拯救。

巴基斯坦基督徒经常面临暴力,他们生活在法律之下,使得难以分享福音. 祈求他们的安全,让他们大胆分享信仰. 祈祷来自伊斯兰背景的信徒在信仰上得到加强,并受到基督兄弟姐妹的鼓励,因为许多人会失去家人和朋友.

祈求激进组织合作, 目的是鼓励他们,训练他们了解圣经,并让他们在穆斯林中接受福音传道。 这些信徒通过圣经研究,教义和一对一的咨询得到训练并得到加强.

在我们祈祷看到教堂在巴基斯坦发展的时候,我们也祈祷下一代的教会领袖和信徒能够拥有坚实的基础和福音传道技巧.

title: Praying for Hindus during Diwali
summary: Jamie Dean provides four prayer points for reaching Hindu communities with the hope of the gospel during Diwali.
summary_zh: 杰米·迪恩（ Jamie Dean ）提供了四个祈祷点，以帮助印度教社区在排灯节期间获得福音的希望。
title_zh: 排灯节期间为印度教徒祈祷
content: On Sunday, Nov. 8, nearly 1.2 billion Hindus worldwide will celebrate Diwali, the most significant holiday in Hinduism each year. More than a billion of those Hindus live in India , making Diwali a massive festival in the world’s most populous (and most Hindu) nation. India also has the world’s largest diaspora population, with an estimated 35 million people living outside the country. During the holiday known as “the festival of lights,” here are a few ways for Christians to pray for the light of Christ to break through Hinduism’s spiritual darkness, whether in India, other nations, or in the lives of our own neighbors: 1. Pray for opportunities to hear and respond to the gospel in India. Many people in India live and die without ever hearing the gospel clearly explained. Pray more Indians will be exposed to the good news of redemption in Christ, and that God will draw many to himself. 2. Pray for Christ-centered churches in India. Though Christians make up only 2 percent of India’s population, that’s still about 28 million people. Pray for faithful, Christ-centered churches to preach the gospel faithfully and reach those around them. 3. Pray for Christians facing persecution to be a faithful witness. Christians in many parts of India face increasing opposition and persecution for their faith in Christ. Pray the Lord will protect these believers and help them to be a faithful witness—including during Diwali, when many Christians stand out for not participating in the holiday. 4. Pray for Hindus in other nations, and in your own neighborhood. Diwali is also a major holiday in other countries, including Nepal , where the majority of the population is Hindu. Pray for Nepalese living in spiritual darkness to hear the gospel of Christ, even as they continue recovering from devastating floods . Pray also for the Indian diaspora. Pray the Lord will give Hindus living in other nations the opportunity to hear the gospel, perhaps for the first time. Pray and look for opportunities in your own city or neighborhood to build friendships that might lead to gospel conversations with Hindu neighbors.

title: Prison Didn’t Mean Paul Was Wrong
summary: Steven Morales explains why following Jesus is worth every sacrifice, even when faithfulness leads to suffering and imprisonment.
summary_zh: 史蒂文·莫拉莱斯（ Steven Morales ）解释了为什么即使忠诚导致痛苦和监禁，跟随耶稣也是值得的。
title_zh: 监狱并不意味着保罗错了
content: “I therefore, a prisoner for the Lord, urge you to walk in a manner worthy of the calling to which you have been called.” (Eph. 4:1) Those are weighty words. And they’re weighty not because Paul is writing from a quiet study or a place of comfort, but because he is writing them from a prison cell. Paul isn’t sending this letter from a position of safety or success as the world defines it. He’s writing as a man in chains—arrested for preaching the gospel and planting churches. To his critics, he was a troublemaker. A dangerous agitator. To God, he was a faithful servant . That matters. Paul is suffering for the very message he’s urging the church in Ephesus to remember and live out. His words carry weight because his life backs them up. He’s not asking them to do anything he himself isn’t already doing—at great personal cost. And here’s the remarkable thing about Paul: there is no scenario in which he loses. Let him go free, and he’ll travel to the ends of the earth preaching Christ and starting churches. Lock him up, and he’ll become “a prisoner for the Lord,” turning his suffering into a living testimony of the worth of the gospel. Execute him? Fine. As he says elsewhere, “For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Phil. 1:21, ESV). There is no situation where Paul says, “The gospel isn’t enough anymore.” There is no moment where he concludes, “This just isn’t worth it.” Instead, Paul’s entire life—especially his suffering—testifies to this truth: no matter your circumstances, trusting in the gospel is never wasted. Paul wasn’t in prison because his ministry failed. He was in prison because he believed the message was worth suffering for. And that’s an important distinction. If a message isn’t worth suffering for, it’s probably not worth believing in. Christianity doesn’t promise a life without pain. What it promises is something better: a suffering that is not meaningless. A hope that suffering does not get the final word. That’s why Paul can say this in 2 Corinthians: “For this light momentary affliction is preparing for us an eternal weight of glory beyond all comparison, as we look not to the things that are seen but to the things that are unseen. For the things that are seen are transient, but the things that are unseen are eternal.” (2 Co. 4:17–18) The gospel gives us a framework for enduring temporary suffering because it anchors us in permanent promises. We can endure hardship now because we know it won’t last forever. Our pain has an expiration date . Why? Because Jesus has already suffered fully in our place. He took sin, death, and judgment upon himself—and walked out of the grave victorious. Because of him, not even death has the final say over us. So when Paul urges believers to “walk in a manner worthy of the calling,” he’s not laying a burden on their shoulders. He’s inviting them into a life shaped by hope—a life that knows that whatever it costs to follow Jesus, it will never be in vain.
